## Abstract

We study the problem of recovering low-dimensional latent geometry from a random geometric graph generated by noisy, high-dimensional data. Specifically, we analyze the performance of a spectral embedding algorithm on the Signal+Noise Graph Model, in which vertices are associated to points perturbed by Gaussian noise, and edges are included for pairs whose inner product exceeds a specified alignment threshold. In the high-dimensional regime where the number $n$ of points and the ambient dimension $d$ both tend to infinity, we show that under a spectral gap condition, the top eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the graph’s adjacency matrix can be used to approximately recover the point cloud up to an orthogonal transformation. We illustrate our results on point clouds sampled from nested spheres and high-dimensional sinusoid curves.

## 1. Introduction

Recovering low-dimensional geometric structure from high-dimensional, noisy data is a fundamental problem in modern data science. Large datasets are often hypothesized to lie near low-dimensional manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, but observations are typically corrupted by noise. Some standard approaches to this problem build an affinity or kernel matrix from the data and extract coordinates via spectral decomposition, as in classical Multidimensional Scaling (MDS), kernel PCA, Laplacian eigenmaps, and diffusion maps. These methods generally require the kernel to be continuous and the data to be densely sampled.

The vast majority of analysis of these algorithms has been under the manifold hypothesis, that the data lies exactly on the low-dimensional manifold, i.e. there is no high-dimensional noise. In this setting, affinity matrices – which may be viewed as Laplacian matrices for weighted graphs with the data points as vertices – have been shown to converge, in various senses, to the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the manifold, at rates depending on the intrinsic dimension [27, 16, 11]. In the high-dimensional additive-noise setting, much less is known. The works [20, 8] quantify how adding noise to a signal affects the spectrum of a kernel or graph Laplacian matrix. The work [7] analyzes an embedding algorithm constructed from the spectral decomposition of a kernel matrix, with kernel function satisfying some regularity hypotheses.

A separate body of work has studied latent space random graph models, in which vertices $i$ are associated to random elements $y_{i}$ of a set $\mathcal{L}$ of “labels” (or “latent features”). Conditional on the labels $(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})$ , each pair $\{i,j\}$ is included as an edge independently with probability $q(y_{i},y_{j})$ , for a fixed affinity function $q:\mathcal{L}^{2}\to[0,1]$ . A central problem is to determine conditions under which the labels $y_{i}$ can be (approximately) recovered from an observation of the graph, with high probability. The most well-studied examples are Stochastic Block Models (SBM), in which $\mathcal{L}$ is a set of fixed cardinality $k$ , inducing a random partition of the vertex set $[n]$ into $k$ communities. In certain parameter ranges there is an information-computation gap, where recovery of the communities is possible, but cannot be achieved by any polynomial-time algorithm. We refer to the [1] for a thorough review of these and related results for SBMs.

Random geometric graphs (RGGs) are a special class of latent space models in which $\mathcal{L}$ is equipped with a metric $\rho$ , and $q$ takes the form $q(x,y)=1_{\rho(x,y)\leq r}$ for a threshold parameter $r$ ; when $\mathcal{L}$ has a Hilbert space structure one may alternatively take $q$ of the form $q(x,y)=1_{\langle x,y\rangle\geq t}$ . Classically, RGGs have been studied for the case that $\mathcal{L}$ is a Euclidean space of fixed dimension [26]. The influential work [4] studied the following hypothesis testing problem for the case that the dimension $d$ grows with the number of vertices $n$ , and the latent points $y_{i}$ are drawn independently and uniformly from the unit sphere $\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ : for what range of $d=d(n)$ is an RGG distinguishable with high probability from an Erdős–Rényi graph of the same expected edge density $p$ ? Results from [4] motivated further progress and a general conjecture in [22] that the models are distinguishable for $d=o((nh(p))^{3})$ and indistinguishable when $d=\omega((nh(p))^{3})$ , where $h(p)$ is the binary entropy function. A proof in the affirmative for the case $d>n$ has recently appeared in [9].

In [21] Li and Schramm introduce the Gaussian Mixture Block Model (GMBM), a random geometric graph in which labels $y_{i}$ are sampled independently from a mixture of two Gaussians on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ centered at $\pm\mu e_{1}$ (on the first coordinate axis). Decomposing $y_{i}=x_{i}+z_{i}$ for $x_{i}$ uniform in $\{+\mu e_{1},-\mu e_{1}\}$ and $z_{i}$ independent Gaussian noise, we can view $x_{i}$ as a clean signal and $z_{i}$ as noise. They establish bounds on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) $\mu$ under which (a) the noisy data $(y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ and (b) the uncorrupted labels $(x_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ can be recovered with high probability from the graph. Their recovery algorithm is based on the spectral decomposition of the graph adjacency matrix. It was recently shown in [15] that exact recovery of the labels $x_{i}$ can be achieved with high probability using a semidefinite program.

In this work, we extend the problem of high-dimensional data recovery from a geometric graph to a more general data model. We introduce the Signal+Noise Graph Model (SNGM) – see Definition 2.1 – in which edges are determined by thresholding inner products for points $y_{i}=x_{i}+z_{i}$ obtained by perturbing an arbitrary random or deterministic point cloud $(x_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ by independent Gaussian noise $(z_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ . Our main result, Theorem 2.5, provides conditions under which an algorithm based on the spectral decomposition of the graph adjacency matrix succeeds in approximately recovering the clean point cloud $(x_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ up to a global orthogonal transformation. We apply this result in Theorem 2.16 to point clouds sampled from a distribution having numerically low-rank population covariance matrix, verifying that natural geometric objects, such as spheres, high-dimensional sinusoid curves with well-separated frequencies, satisfy the required regularity conditions.

This construction generalizes the GMBM framework of Li and Schramm from a two-component mixture to a numerically low-rank geometric signal. The resulting adjacency matrix in the GMBM setup is effectively a non-linear, discontinuous, spiked kernel random matrix. From this perspective, our work connects the study of high-dimensional RGGs to the broader theory of spiked random matrix models. In the null setting where there is no underlying signal, the spectrum of kernel random matrices generated from isotropic data have been analyzed in [13, 5, 23, 10], with limiting spectral distributions described by deterministic laws. Approximate recovery of isotropic data was studied in [14, 2, 25], and the recent work [24] considers anisotropic Gaussian data $y_{i}\sim N(0,\Sigma)$ . In the spiked setting, [17] studies non-linear Wigner spiked models with continuous kernels, identifying signal-to-noise thresholds for eigenvector alignment.

Apart from [21], the work most closely related to the present work is [7], which studies an embedding algorithm for noisy data based on the spectral decomposition of a kernel matrix. The main differences are: (i) [7] considers a smooth kernel function with a scaling that yields a dense kernel matrix, whereas our kernel function is a discontinuous indicator yielding a potentially very sparse matrix; (ii) their data model takes the clean data $x_{i}$ to be i.i.d. samples from a continuous distribution on a low-dimensional sub-manifold, whereas our results apply to full-rank deterministic point clouds; (iii) on the other hand, while we restrict to Gaussian noise, [7] considers general isotropic sub-Gaussian noise.

Our framework relaxes the strict low-rank assumption common in the spiked random matrix literature. Rather than requiring the clean signal data to lie exactly in a $k$ -dimensional subspace we allow that the principal components grow with $n,d$ , provided the tail singular values decay sufficiently fast and no individual point dominates the cloud’s structure.

### 1.1. Notation

An index of notation is provided in Appendix B.

Asymptotic notation. $C,c,C_{0}$ etc. denote positive absolute constants. For two sequences $a_{n},b_{n}$ , we write $\omega(a_{n})=b_{n}$ or $a_{n}=o(b_{n})$ if $\lim_{n\to\infty}|a_{n}/b_{n}|=0$ . We use $\tilde{\omega}(a_{n})=b_{n}$ and $a_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny log}}}{{\ll}}b_{n}$ to indicate that $b_{n}\geq a_{n}\log^{C}n$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$ . We write $a=O(b)$ or $a\lesssim b$ to mean there exists some constant $C>0$ such that $|a|\leq C\cdot b$ , and $a_{n}\lessapprox b_{n}$ if $|a_{n}|\leq b_{n}\cdot\log^{C}n$ . We also write $a_{n}=\Theta(b_{n})$ to indicate that there exists $n_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ such that $a_{n}\lesssim b_{n}\lesssim a_{n}$ for all $n>n_{0}$ . Similarly, we use $a_{n}\asymp b_{n}$ to indicate that $a_{n}\lesssim b_{n}\lesssim a_{n}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ .

Linear algebra. We denote the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ by $\mathcal{S}^{m-1}$ . For a symmetric matrix $B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ , we denote its eigenvalues by $\lambda_{1}(B)\geq\dots\geq\lambda_{n}(B)$ . The singular values of a rectangular matrix $B$ are denoted $\sigma_{i}(B):=\lambda_{i}(B^{\mathsf{T}}B)^{1/2}$ . We denote the spectral operator norm by $\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ and the Frobenius norm by $\|B\|_{F}$ . For any matrix $B$ , let $\Pi_{B}^{(k)}$ denote the orthogonal projection matrix onto the subspace spanned by the top $k$ eigenvectors of $BB^{\mathsf{T}}$ . We use the notation $\odot$ to denote the Hadamard (entrywise) product between two matrices of the same dimension. The operator $\diag$ is context dependent, for a matrix $B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ , $\diag(B)$ , it zeros out the off-diagonal entries of $B$ , whereas for scalars $a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\in\mathbb{R}$ , $\diag(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})$ it creates a diagonal matrix.

## 2. Model setup and results

### 2.1. The Model

To study the extent to which high-dimensional data can be recovered from binary information on pairwise alignment of data points after corruption by additive noise, we introduce to the following general random graph model.

#### Definition 2.1 (Signal+Noise Graph Model (SNGM)).

Given a ‘clean’ point cloud $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and edge-density parameter $p\in[0,1]$ , the Signal+Noise Graph Model (SNGM) is a distribution over $n$ -vertex graphs $G\sim\mathcal{G}_{n,d}(p,\mathcal{X})$ generated as follows:

- • Independently sample Gaussian vectors $z_{1},\dots,z_{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})$ , and set $y_{i}:=x_{i}+z_{i}$ .

- • Let $V(G)=[n]$ , and add an edge $\{i,j\}$ to $E(G)$ if and only if $\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau$ , where $\tau(p,n,d,\mathcal{X})$ is taken such that (2.1)

$$ \frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}\sum_{i<j}\mathbb{P}\left(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)=p\,. $$

We denote by $X,Y,Z$ the $n\times d$ matrices with rows $x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}},y_{i}^{\mathsf{T}},z_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}$ , respectively, and $\Sigma:=\frac{1}{n}X^{\mathsf{T}}X$ the sample covariance matrix for the clean point cloud.

#### Remark 2.2 (GMBM as a special case of the SNGM).

The GMBM of [21] is recovered by taking $x_{i}$ i.i.d. and uniform from $\{-\mu e_{1},\mu e_{1}\}$ , independent of the noise $Z$ , so that $\Sigma=\mu^{2}e_{1}e_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}$ is rank one and the noisy data $y_{i}$ encodes a symmetric and centered two-community structure.

#### Remark 2.3 (Colored noise).

Our results below admit straightforward extensions to the more general setup that $z_{i}$ are iid centered Gaussian vectors with invertible covariance matrix $\frac{1}{d}C$ . Indeed, our main result Theorem 2.5 extends as written to allow any $C$ satisfying $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}},\|C^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ , by multiplying the data $X$ on the right by $C^{-1/2}$ to reduce to the white noise case $C=I_{d}$ .

#### Remark 2.4.

In the context of latent space graph models, the vectors that dictate the edge formation ( $y_{i}$ in this case) would traditionally be referred to as latent vectors. However, to clearly distinguish the underlying clean point cloud $\mathcal{X}$ from the noisy samples $\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ in our model, we will refer to $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ as clean and noisy vectors (or points), respectively.

### 2.2. Spectral embedding algorithm

We analyze the following spectral algorithm to approximately recover a point cloud (up to a global orthogonal transformation) from a geometric graph $G$ generated from noisy measurements of a point cloud $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . The algorithm returns a point cloud $\mathcal{X}^{G}=\{x_{1}^{G},\dots,x_{n}^{G}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{k}$ that one hopes retains approximately the same metric structure as $\mathcal{X}$ .

Inputs: A graph $G$ over vertex set $[n]$ and integers $k,d\in[n]$ with $k\leq d$ . (1) Compute the edge density $\hat{p}=\hat{p}(G):=\binom{n}{2}^{-1}|E(G)|$ . (2) Compute eigenpairs $\{\eta_{i},\mathbf{w}_{i}\}^{k}_{i=1}$ of the $n\times n$ adjacency matrix $A$ , where $A_{ij}=\1[\{i,j\}\in E(G)]$ , and eigenvalues are labeled $\eta_{0}\geq\dots\geq\eta_{n-1}$ . (3) Output: rows $x_{1}^{G},\dots,x_{n}^{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ of the $n\times k$ embedding matrix (2.2)

$$ X_{G}:=\sqrt{\alpha(\hat{p})}\mathbf{W}_{k}D_{k}^{1/2} $$

where $\mathbf{W}_{k}=[\mathbf{w}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{w}_{k}]$ , $D_{k}:=(\max(\eta_{i},0))_{i=1}^{k}$ , and we define a scaling function (2.3)

$$ \alpha:(0,1)\to\mathbb{R}^{+},\qquad\alpha(q):=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{d-k}}\exp\bigg(\frac{d-k}{2d}\Psi^{-1}(q)^{2}\bigg) $$

with $\Psi(t):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{t}^{\infty}e^{-s^{2}/2}ds$ the complementary distribution function of a Gaussian.

Note that since the input graph for the algorithm depends on the data only through inner products, one can only hope to recover the point cloud up to a global orthogonal transformation. Hence, we will evaluate the performance of the approximation through recovery of the Gram matrix $XX^{\mathsf{T}}=(\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle)_{i,j=1}^{n}$ .

The parameter $k$ is an estimate for the effective rank of the clean data matrix $X$ . The above algorithm treats $k$ as an input, but if it is unknown then it can be selected in step 2 based on a gap in the spectrum of $A$ .

### 2.3. Main result

Our main technical result is the following theorem, showing that the spectral embedding algorithm of Section 2.2 performs well on the SNGM (Definition 2.1) under suitable hypotheses. Recall our conventions for asymptotic notation from Section 1.1.

#### Theorem 2.5.

Suppose that $n,d\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ , $p\geq 0$ satisfy

$$ \omega(\log^{16}n)\leq d<n\,,\qquad\omega\bigg(\frac{\log^{18}n}{n}\bigg)\leq p\leq 0.49\,. $$

Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ such that

$$ \frac{1}{n}\|X\|_{F}^{2}=\Tr\Sigma\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n} $$

with rows $x_{1}^{\mathsf{T}},\dots,x_{n}^{\mathsf{T}}$ satisfying

$$ \max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\frac{1}{n}\|X\|_{F}^{2}\,. $$

Denoting by $\mu_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\mu_{d}\geq 0$ the singular values of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}X$ , assume

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{k} \displaystyle\geq\omega(d^{-1/2})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{2}=o\left(\min(d^{-1},p^{3})\right), $$

for some integer $k$ . If $G\sim\mathcal{G}_{n,d}(p,\mathcal{X})$ , then for $X_{G}$ as in (2.2), with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lessapprox\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X):=\frac{n\mu_{1}}{\sqrt{d}}+\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\left(n\sqrt{d}\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr\Sigma+\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}+\frac{n}{p\sqrt{d}}\Big(\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{2}\Big)^{1/4}\right)\,. $$

We will first prove Theorem 2.5 in the special case that the clean data matrix $X$ is of rank $k$ , in which case

$$ \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)=\frac{n\mu_{1}}{\sqrt{d}}+\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\left(n\sqrt{d}\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr\Sigma+\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}\right)\,. $$

See Theorem 4.1. Since $\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=n\mu_{1}^{2}$ , from (2.9) we see that in the rank- $k$ case, we guarantee a relative error $\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}/\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=o(1)$ when, for instance,

$$ d\lessapprox np\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mu_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny log}}}{{\gg}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny log}}}{{\gg}}\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\Tr\Sigma, $$

where $a\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny log}}}{{\gg}}b$ means $a\geq b\cdot\log^{C}n$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$ . (One can relax one of the implicit polylogarithmic factors by tightening another.)

#### Remark 2.6 (On the Implicit polylogarithmic Factors).

See Section 4 for refined bounds with explicit logarithmic factors, which we have not attempted to optimize.

#### Remark 2.7.

Our hypotheses imply that $k=o(\sqrt{d}/\log^{2}n)$ . Indeed, from the bounds in (2.5), (2.7) it follows $\omega(\frac{k}{d})\leq k\mu^{2}_{k}\leq\Tr\Sigma\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}$ .

#### Remark 2.8.

The upper bound of 0.49 in (2.4) could be replaced by any fixed number less than $\frac{1}{2}$ .

As a consequence of Theorem 2.5 we obtain conditions under which the embedding $X_{G}$ recovers most of the dot products $\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle$ with vanishing error.

#### Corollary 2.9.

With $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)$ as in (2.8), let

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{F}(X) \displaystyle:=\sqrt{k}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)+n\Big(\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{4}\Big)^{1/2} \displaystyle=n\sqrt{\frac{k}{d}}\Bigg[\mu_{1}+\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\bigg(d\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr\Sigma+\sqrt{\frac{1}{np}}+\frac{1}{p}\Big(\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{2}\Big)^{1/4}\bigg)\Bigg]+n\Big(\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{4}\Big)^{1/2}. $$

Under the same assumptions as Theorem 2.5, and the same event under which (2.8) holds, we have

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}\lessapprox\mathcal{E}_{F}(X)\,. $$

Moreover, for any $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and a sufficiently large constant $C>0$ , and $x_{i}^{G}$ the $i$ -th rows of $X_{G}$

$$ |\{(i,j):i\neq j,|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle-\langle x_{i}^{G},x_{j}^{G}\rangle|\geq\frac{\log^{C}n}{n\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\mathcal{E}_{F}(X)\}\lvert\leq n^{2}\varepsilon, $$

and

$$ \Bigg\lvert\bigg\{i\in[n]:|\|x_{i}\|^{2}_{2}-\|x_{i}^{G}\|^{2}_{2}|\geq\frac{\log^{C}n}{\varepsilon n}\Big(2k\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)+n\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{2}\Big)\bigg\}\Bigg\rvert\leq\varepsilon n. $$

In particular,

$$ \Bigg\lvert\bigg\{i\in[n]:|\|x_{i}\|_{2}-\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}|\geq\frac{\log^{C/2}n}{\sqrt{\varepsilon n}}\Big(2k\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)+n\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}\bigg\}\Bigg\rvert\leq\varepsilon n\,. $$

#### Remark 2.10 (Relative Recovery).

If one wishes to obtain a relative error statement, implied by (2.11),(2.12), (2.13), this would only be feasible for inner products and norms that are large enough compared to the additive errors in the aforementioned equations. We make such a statement in Corollary 8.1 for “good” sets: samples having large enough inner products and norms.

#### Remark 2.11 (Error terms).

The bound (2.8) is a sum of four contributions. The first term, $n\mu_{1}/\sqrt{d}$ , is the concentration error: it measures how well the top- $k$ eigenspace of the noisy Gram matrix $YY^{\mathsf{T}}$ aligns with that of $XX^{\mathsf{T}}$ once the $d-k$ orthogonal noise coordinates are projected away (Lemma 5.1). The second term $n(\mu_{1}^{4}/\mu_{k}^{2})\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma$ , is the cost of approximating the discontinuous edge indicator by its low-degree Gegenbauer expansion. It grows with the signal magnitude $\Tr\Sigma$ and quantifies the breakdown of the first-order spherical-harmonic approximation when the signal is too large. The third contribution $\mu_{1}^{2}/\mu_{k}^{2}\sqrt{n/(dp)}$ is the density term: if the graph is too sparse there is too little information to recover the geometry. Relative to $\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=n\mu_{1}^{2}$ , this density term is $\mu_{k}^{-2}(ndp)^{-1/2}$ , which is $o(1)$ , provided $\omega(1)\leq d\leq o(np)$ up to polylogarithms. The fourth term $n\mu_{1}^{2}/\mu_{k}^{2}(\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{2})^{1/4}(p\sqrt{d})^{-1}$ is the contribution of the tail end of the spectrum of the point-cloud, it quantifies the cost of estimating data that is not strictly low-dimensional. Moreover, our methods approximate the adjacency matrix of a SNGM by slightly perturbed spherical data. The multiplicative factor of $\mu_{1}^{2}/\mu_{k}^{2}$ can be interpreted as the penalty for having a highly anisotropic point-cloud. Specifically it quantifies how well the assumption (2.6) is met.

#### Remark 2.12 (Sufficient Conditions for Vanishing Error).

Under a strengthening of the hypotheses in Theorem 2.5, the right hand side of the relative operator norm error is $o(1)$ provided that:

- $(i)_{\mathrm{op}}$ $(\mu_{1}/\mu_{k})^{2}\Tr\Sigma=o(d^{-1/2})$ ,

- $(ii)_{\mathrm{op}}$ $np=\omega\big(\frac{1}{\mu_{k}^{4}d}\big)$ .

$\mathcal{E}_{F}$ from Corollary 2.9 is $o(1)$ provided that:

- $(i)_{F}$ $\mu_{k}^{2}\sqrt{d}=\omega(\mu_{1})$ ,

- $(ii)_{F}$ $(\mu_{1}/\mu_{k})^{4}\Tr\Sigma=o(d^{-1/2})$ ,

- $(iii)_{F}$ $np=\omega\big(\frac{\mu_{1}^{4}}{\mu_{k}^{8}d}\big)$ .

The regime $\mu_{1}/\mu_{k}=O(1)$ , satisfies conditions $(i)_{F}$ , $(ii)_{F}$ and $(i)_{\mathrm{op}}$ via $\Tr\Sigma\lesssim 1/(\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n)$ and (2.7). In the hardest case of a critically small, well-conditioned signal ( $\mu_{1}/\mu_{k}=O(1)$ , $\mu_{k}^{2}\asymp 1/d$ ) this means we must have $np=\omega(d)$ . In other words, the average degree must dominate the ambient dimension. Under $(i)_{\mathrm{op}}$ – $(ii)_{\mathrm{op}}$ the spectral embedding recovers $XX^{T}$ up to rotation with relative operator norm error $o(1)$ and Frobenius norm respectively with $(i)_{F}$ – $(iii)_{F}$ . Moreover, in Theorem 2.5, if one wishes for the truncation terms in terms of $\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{2}$ to be $o(1)$ , note that the right-hand side of (4.1) (the $\mu_{k+1}=0$ case) agrees with (2.5) up to an additive factor, thus it suffices to impose the stronger tail decay $\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{2}\leq o(\mu_{k}^{8}p^{4}d^{2})$ . We choose a weaker hypothesis (2.7) that keeps these term explicit.

#### Remark 2.13 (On the assumptions in Theorem 2.5).

$\bullet$ $\Tr\Sigma\leq 1/\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n$ : While it appears counter-intuitive to cap the strength of the signal $\Tr(\Sigma)$ , in general some upper bound is necessary for recovery. Indeed, if the points are too separated in latent space, then the SNGM may be disconnected, in which case it contains no information about the relative position of points in latent space between vertices in distinct disconnected components. We have made no attempt to prove that this is the optimal upper bound. Moreover the proof techniques employed in this paper, rely on representing the adjacency matrix of the SNGM by low-order spherical harmonics, which is a better approximation when the noise and signal are comparable in magnitude. However, this approximation fails for larger signal-to-noise ratios (SNR)- one may expect higher-order harmonics to contribute in the larger SNR regime. Note moreover, that the proof of Theorem 2.5 shows that one can relax this assumption to $\Tr\Sigma\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}$ , but to avoid overcrowding the error with constants, we keep ‘ $\leq$ ’.

$\bullet$ No Outliers: The spherical approximation is why we also have the assumption (2.6), which we refer to as the ‘no outlier’ condition on the clean vectors, in the top $k$ eigenvector directions. We want the most important eigenvectors to be not too far from a sphere in $k$ dimensions for the Gegenbauer approximation to be ‘good’. Hence the ‘no-outlier’ condition on the projected point cloud. Intuitively, by restricting the maximum squared norm of any projected point to be at most a multiple of the average of the norms, we prevent extreme outliers from distorting the underlying projected point cloud.

#### Remark 2.14 (More general kernel functions).

Finally, we note that our arguments apply to more general kernel matrices than the graph adjacency matrix $A$ (for which the kernel function is an indicator) – see (6.6). We limit the presentation to the step kernel function for concreteness.

### 2.4. Applications to randomly sampled point clouds

Definition 2.1 and Theorem 2.5 are stated for a fixed set $\mathcal{X}$ of points in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . In this section we apply our results to data sampled from continuous manifolds.

We begin by proving a generic result for i.i.d. data $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}$ sampled from a distribution $\nu$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with compact support. We do not directly work with assumptions on a manifold, nor do we assume anything further about the distribution $\nu$ that we sample from, but rather we consider $\Sigma^{\infty}$ , the “true” data covariance matrix for $x_{i}$ . To this end, we define the population covariance analogue of $\Sigma=\frac{1}{n}X^{\mathsf{T}}X$ in Definition 2.1,

#### Definition 2.15 (Population distribution).

For a distribution $\nu$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with compact support, we define the population covariance matrix $\Sigma^{\infty}$ by

$$ \Sigma^{\infty}:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. $$

We denote the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\Sigma^{\infty}$ as $(\lambda_{i},u_{i})_{i=1}^{d}$ , where $\lambda_{1}\geq\dots\geq\lambda_{d}$ .

In order to apply Theorem 2.5 to $\mathcal{X}$ , we observe that for large $n$ ,

$$ \Sigma=\frac{1}{n}X^{\mathsf{T}}X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\approx\Sigma^{\infty} $$

by the law of large numbers (the above display will be made precise in Lemma 9.2). Therefore, we can translate our conditions on $\Sigma$ in Theorem 2.5 or Theorem 4.1 to those on $\Sigma^{\infty}$ .

We begin by considering the setting where $\Sigma^{\infty}$ is numerically low rank and an easily applicable Corollary (Theorem 2.16 and Corollary 2.18). We then apply each of these variants to concrete examples that are commonplace in the manifold learning literature. The proofs can be found in Section 9.

#### Theorem 2.16 (Denoising with numerically low-rank $\Sigma^{\infty}$ ).

Let $n,d,p$ be as in Theorem 2.5. Let $X$ be the matrix whose rows are given by the point cloud $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}$ sampled independently from a distribution $\nu$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , with $\omega(\log^{16}n)\leq d<n$ . Moreover, suppose

$$ \Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}=o\bigg(\frac{np^{3}}{\log n}\bigg), $$

$$ \esssup_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}, $$

and that there exists $1\leq k\leq d$ such that

$$ \lambda_{k}=\omega(d^{-1})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\lambda_{j}=o\left(\min(d^{-1},p^{3})\right). $$

Let $G\sim\mathcal{G}_{n,d}(p,\mathcal{X})$ . For the spectral algorithm of Section 2.2, with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lessapprox \displaystyle n\lambda_{1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d\lambda_{1}}}+\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{k}}\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}\sqrt{d}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{np}}+\frac{(\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\lambda_{j})^{1/4}}{p}\right)\right) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\lessapprox\sqrt{k}n\lambda_{1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d\lambda_{1}}}+\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{k}}\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}\sqrt{d}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{np}}+\frac{(\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\lambda_{j})^{1/4}}{p}\right)\right)+\sqrt{\lambda_{k+1}}\sqrt{\sum_{j>k}\lambda_{j}}. $$

#### Remark 2.17.

The second bound in (2.15) follows automatically from the first bound when $d=o(n^{2}p^{6}\log^{2}n)$ .

In practice, verifying assumption (2.17) in Theorem 2.16 can be challenging. However, if $\Sigma^{\infty}$ is approximately diagonal, the diagonal entries of $\Sigma^{\infty}$ serve as proxies for eigenvalues of $\Sigma^{\infty}$ thanks to matrix perturbation inequalities. The corollary below handles this case explicitly, allowing for an arbitrary perturbation of order $O(1/d)$ . We will illustrate the utility of this corollary in an application to a high-dimensional sinusoid curve in Section 2.5.3.

#### Corollary 2.18 (Denoising with approximately diagonal $\Sigma^{\infty}$ ).

Let $X$ be the matrix whose rows are given by the point cloud $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}$ sampled from a compactly supported distribution $\nu$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , with $\omega(\log^{16}n)\leq d<n$ and $\Sigma^{\infty}=\text{\emph{Diag}}(\Sigma^{\infty})+E$ where $\|E\|_{\text{\emph{op}}}\lesssim\frac{1}{d}$ . Without loss of generality assume $\Sigma^{\infty}_{11}\geq\Sigma^{\infty}_{22}\geq\ldots\geq\Sigma^{\infty}_{dd}$ . Moreover, suppose

$$ \Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}=o\bigg(\frac{np^{3}}{\log n}\bigg), $$

$$ \esssup_{x\sim\nu}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=O(\Tr(\Sigma^{\infty})), $$

and there exists $k$ such that

$$ \Sigma^{\infty}_{kk}=\omega(d^{-1})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}=o\left(\min(d^{-1},p^{3})\right). $$

Let $G\sim\mathcal{G}_{n,d}(p,\mathcal{X})$ with $pn\geq\omega(\log^{18}(n))$ . If we apply the spectral algorithm (Section 2.2) with $k$ as chosen above then with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lessapprox n\Sigma^{\infty}_{11}\Bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d\Sigma^{\infty}_{11}}}+\frac{\Sigma^{\infty}_{11}}{\Sigma^{\infty}_{kk}}\sqrt{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}+\frac{1}{\Sigma^{\infty}_{kk}\sqrt{d}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{np}}+\frac{(\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj})^{1/4}}{p}\right)\Bigg). $$

#### Remark 2.19 (Recovery for randomly sampled point clouds).

Since these bounds are expressed through $\Sigma^{\infty}$ rather than $\Sigma$ and can be made more specific depending on their applications, it is more natural to state recovery guarantees on a case-to-case basis, such as in Propositions 2.20, 2.22, 2.25, and 9.7.

### 2.5. Examples

Here we apply the results of the previous subsection to signals sampled from a compact manifold, such as: spheres (Proposition 2.20) and their nested mixtures (Proposition 2.22) and sinusoidal curves (Proposition 2.25).

#### 2.5.1. Sphere in $m$ dimensions

Let $s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}$ be i.i.d. samples from the sphere of radius $R$ in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . Let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ be the $d$ -dimensional vectors obtained by extending each $s_{i}$ with $d-m$ zero entries.

#### Proposition 2.20.

In the above setting, if $np=\omega(1)$ , $\omega(\frac{m}{d})\leq R^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny log}}}{{\ll}}d^{-1/2}$ , and $\omega(\log^{16}n)=d<n$ , then for $X_{G}$ as in (2.2) with $k=m$ , with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \frac{\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\lessapprox\frac{\sqrt{m}}{R\sqrt{d}}+\sqrt{d}R^{2}+\frac{m}{R^{2}\sqrt{npd}}, $$

and the same bound holds for $(\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F})/\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}$ .

Moreover, if additionally

$$ R^{2}\sqrt{npd}=\tilde{\omega}(m)\qquad\text{and, }\qquad\tilde{\omega}(\frac{m}{d})=R^{2}\lessapprox\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, $$

then with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ we have

$$ |\{i:\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}=(1+o(1))R\}|=(1-o(1))n\,, $$

and for any fixed $\varepsilon_{0}\in(0,\frac{1}{8}]$ ,

$$ |\{(i,j):i\neq j,\langle x_{i}^{G},x_{j}^{G}\rangle=(1+o_{\varepsilon_{0}}(1))\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\}|\geq\bigg(1-2\varepsilon_{0}-\frac{1}{m}-o(1)\bigg)\bigg)n(n-1)\,. $$

#### Remark 2.21.

In the additional assumptions e.g (2.25), the implicit polylog factors are chosen according to the hidden polylogs in Proposition 2.20, and are made more precise in the proofs of the statements.

#### 2.5.2. Mixture of nested spheres

Here we generalize the previous example to a mixture of nested spheres. More precisely, for $1\leq j\leq s$ , let $\mathbb{P}_{j}\sim\text{Unif}(R_{j}\mathcal{S}^{m-1})$ for $R_{j}>0$ and $w_{j}>0$ such that $\sum_{j=1}^{s}w_{j}=1$ . Then,

$$ x_{i}\sim\sum_{j=1}^{s}w_{j}\mathbb{P}_{j}, $$

i.e. with probability $w_{j}$ we draw $x_{i}$ from $\mathbb{P}_{j}$ . For convenience, without loss of generality we assume that $R_{1}<R_{2}<\ldots<R_{s}$ .

#### Proposition 2.22.

Suppose $\mathcal{X}$ is sampled from a mixture of nested spheres as described above. Let $R^{2}\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{s}R_{j}^{2}w_{j}$ . If $np=\omega(1)$ , $\omega(\frac{m}{d})=R^{2}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}$ , $R_{s}^{2}=O(R^{2})$ and $\omega(\log^{16}n)=d<n$ , then with probability at least (2.24) holds, and the same bound holds for the relative Frobenius norm error.

A natural question is whether the vectors in the embedding associated to distinct spheres remain well separated. For an appropriate choice of model parameters, the answer is “yes”, as stated below.

#### Proposition 2.23.

Consider $\mathcal{X}$ as in Proposition 2.22. Additionally, assume that for some constant $C_{0}>0$ , $\frac{R}{C_{0}}\leq R_{j}\leq C_{0}R$ and $\frac{1}{C_{0}}\leq w_{j}$ for all $j\in[s]$ . Let $\alpha=\min_{j\in[s]}(R_{j}-R_{j-1})$ with $R_{0}=0$ and $x_{i}^{G}$ denote the $i$ th row of $X_{G}$ . Moreover, assume $\tilde{\omega}(\frac{m}{d})=R^{2}$ , $\tilde{\omega}(R^{2})=d^{-1/2}$ and $R^{2}\sqrt{npd}=\tilde{\omega}(m)$ . Then there exists $\beta>0$ such that if for some $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ ,

$$ \alpha=\omega_{C_{0}}\bigg(\frac{R}{\varepsilon_{0}\log^{\beta}n}\bigg) $$

then

$$ |\{i:|\|x_{i}\|_{2}-\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}|=o(\alpha)\text{\emph{ and }}|\|x_{i}\|_{2}-\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}|=o_{C_{0}}(\|x_{i}\|_{2})\}|\geq(1-\varepsilon_{0})n, $$

with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ .

#### Remark 2.24.

In words, the above result shows that under appropriate conditions, if $x_{i}$ is sampled from $R_{j}\mathcal{S}^{m-1}$ then $x_{i}^{G}$ lies much closer to $R_{j}\mathcal{S}^{m-1}$ than any other $R_{j^{\prime}}\mathcal{S}^{m-1}$ , meaning, the spectral embedding recovers the separation between distinct spheres by approximately preserving signal vector lengths.

#### 2.5.3. Sinusoid curve

Unlike the spheres and nested spheres, a sinusoid curve can be constructed such that it has a numerically low-rank population covariance matrix, rather than a strictly low rank one. Moreover, here we consider a convenient choice of curve parameters that make the population covariance matrix diagonal to leading order, which places this example in the setting of Corollary 2.18.

#### Proposition 2.25 (Sinusoid curve).

Suppose $\omega(\log^{16}n)=d<n$ . Let $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}$ with $x_{j}=\big(a_{i}\cos(\omega_{i}T_{j}+\phi_{i})\big)_{i=1}^{d}$ , where $T_{1},\dots,T_{n}$ are independent and uniform in $[0,1]$ , and the $a_{i},\omega_{i},\phi_{i}$ are deterministic. Suppose the amplitudes and frequencies satisfy

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}=o\bigg(\frac{np^{3}}{\log n}\bigg), $$

and, with $a_{1}\geq\dots\geq a_{d}\geq 0$ , that there exists $1\leq k\leq d$ such that

$$ \sum_{j>k}^{d}a_{j}^{2}=o\bigg(\min(d^{-1},p^{3})\bigg), $$

$$ a_{k}^{2}=\omega(d^{-1}), $$

and,

$$ \Omega:=\min_{i\neq j}||\omega_{i}|-|\omega_{j}||\gtrsim|a_{1}|^{2}d^{2},\qquad\min_{i}|\omega_{i}|\gtrsim 1\,. $$

Then for $G\sim\mathcal{G}_{n,d}(p,\mathcal{X})$ with $pn=\omega(\log^{18}n)$ , applying the spectral algorithm with this choice of $k$ gives, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lessapprox n\frac{a_{1}}{\sqrt{d}}+n\frac{a_{1}^{4}}{a_{k}^{2}}\sqrt{d}\sum^{d}_{j=1}a_{j}^{2}+n\frac{a_{1}^{2}}{a_{k}^{2}\sqrt{d}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{np}}+\frac{(\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}a_{j}^{2})^{1/4}}{p}\right), $$

and Frobenius norm error

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\lessapprox\sqrt{k}\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_{k}^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{l>k}^{d}a_{j}^{2}}. $$

Suppose additionally that

$$ a_{1}/a_{k}=O(1),\qquad k=\omega(1), $$

and that,

$$ \sum_{j=k+1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}=o\big(p^{4}/d^{2}\big),\qquad np\geq\omega(d). $$

Then on the same event on which (2.34) holds, we have that with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \big|\big\{i\in[n]:\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}=(1+o(1))\|x_{i}\|_{2}\big\}\big|=(1-o(1))n. $$

#### Remark 3.1 (On the Numerical Implementation).

The numerical experiments presented in this section are intended primarily as qualitative proofs of concept to motivate the theoretical framework. Developing an optimized, practical implementation of this spectral algorithm falls outside the scope of the present work. As established in our main results, the theoretical error bounds contain several implicit constants and polylogarithmic factors that we haven’t optimized for in our proofs. Consequently, identifying the optimal hyper-parameters (e.g., the optimal edge density $p$ or the exact ambient dimension scaling) to minimize the empirical error in finite-sample regimes is a non-trivial task, which depends on the data distribution. A comprehensive empirical study dedicated to fine-tuning these parameters for practical manifold recovery may require additional work.

## 4. Proof overviews

For clarity of presentation, we will first establish Theorem 2.5 in the special case that the clean data matrix $X$ is of rank $k$ , i.e. $\mu_{i}=0$ for $k+1\leq i\leq d$ . We state this result as Theorem 4.1 below, which we note makes a milder assumption on the density $p$ . The extension to the full-rank setting is carried out in Section 7.

#### Theorem 4.1 (Spectral recovery for low-rank point clouds).

Suppose that $n,d\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ , $p\geq 0$ satisfy

$$ \omega(\log^{16}n)\leq d<n\,,\qquad\omega\bigg(\frac{\log^{2}n}{n}\bigg)\leq p\leq\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon\, $$

for some fixed $\epsilon>0$ . Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ satisfy (2.5) and (2.6), and assume

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{k} \displaystyle\geq\omega(d^{-1/2})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mu_{k+1}=0 $$

for some integer $k$ . If $G\sim\mathcal{G}_{n,d}(p,\mathcal{X})$ , then for $X_{G}$ as in (2.2), with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lessapprox\frac{n\mu_{1}}{\sqrt{d}}+\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\left(n\sqrt{d}\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr\Sigma+\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}\right)\,. $$

The proof of Theorem 4.1 breaks into three comparisons, accomplished by Lemma 4.2, Proposition 4.3 and Proposition 4.4 below, the proofs of which are deferred to subsequent sections.

As a first step, it will be convenient for the analysis to replace the scaling factor $\alpha(\hat{p})$ in (2.2) with a quantity that is based on the model parameter $p$ (or equivalently, the inner product threshold $\tau$ from (2.1)) rather than the estimated edge density $\hat{p}$ . We can do this because the latter concentrates around the former. Recalling $\tau$ from (2.1), set

$$ p_{1}:=\mathbb{E}u_{1}\1(u_{1}\geq\tau)\,, $$

for $u=(u_{1},\dots,u_{d-k})$ uniform on $\mathcal{S}^{d-k-1}$ . (See (A.11) for a more cumbersome explicit formula.) With $\mathbf{W}_{k},D_{k}$ as in Section 2.2, set

$$ \hat{X}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(d-k)p_{1}}}\mathbf{W}_{k}D_{k}^{1/2}\,. $$

Noting that the scaling parameter $\alpha(\hat{p})$ from (2.3) can be expressed as

$$ \alpha(\hat{p})=\frac{1}{(d-k)\hat{p}_{1}}\qquad\text{for }\quad\hat{p}_{1}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi(d-k)}}\,e^{-(d-k)\hat{\tau}^{2}/2} $$

we see that

$$ X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}=\frac{p_{1}}{\hat{p}_{1}}\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}. $$

The following lemma thus allows us to pass from $X_{G}$ to $\hat{X}$ .

#### Lemma 4.2.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 2.5, with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \frac{\hat{p}_{1}}{p_{1}}=1+O\Big(\sqrt{\log(1/p)}\Big(\mathcal{E}_{1}+\sqrt{\tfrac{\log n}{np}}\Big)\Big) $$

where $\mathcal{E}_{1}=\mathcal{E}_{1}(X):=\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma+(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n+\frac{\log^{2}n}{\sqrt{d}}$ .

We prove Lemma 4.2 in Section A.5.

Having reduced to comparing $XX^{\mathsf{T}}$ with $\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}$ , our next proposition controls the difference between these in terms of the error for a spectral approximation $\hat{Y}$ to the noisy data matrix $Y$ . Recalling the labeling $\eta_{0}\geq\cdots\geq\eta_{n-1}$ for the eigenvalues of $A$ , with $(\mathbf{w}_{j})_{j=0}^{n-1}$ denoting a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, we set11 1 Note that we in fact only define the Gram matrix $\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ and do not define $\hat{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ itself. While it can be shown that $\eta_{d}>0$ with high probability for $d=o(n)$ , so that $\hat{Y}$ could be defined similarly to $\hat{X}$ in (4.5), we only ever work with $\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ , with slight abuse of notation to remind the reader that it is an approximation for $YY^{\mathsf{T}}$ .

$$ \hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}:=\frac{1}{(d-k)p_{1}}\mathbf{W}_{d}D_{d}\mathbf{W}_{d}^{\mathsf{T}} $$

where $\mathbf{W}_{d}=[\mathbf{w}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{w}_{d}]$ and $D_{d}:=\diag(\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{d})$ .

#### Proposition 4.3.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.1, with probability $1-O(e^{-\sqrt{d}})$ ,

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n\mu_{1}}{\sqrt{d}}+\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

We prove Proposition 4.3 in Section 5, using concentration properties of the Gaussian noise and perturbation inequalities for eigenvalues and spectral projections.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.1, with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \big\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\sqrt{d}\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma)\log^{4}(n)+\left(n\frac{\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}{d^{3/2}}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}\right)\log^{9}n+\log^{4}n. $$

where in the penultimate line we noted that our assumptions (2.4)–(2.6) and $\mu_{k}=\omega(d^{-1/2})$ imply that the error expression $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ from Lemma 4.2 is $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma)$ , and that the right hand side of (4.10) is $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{d}\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr\Sigma+\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}))$ , and in the final line we noted that the term $\mu_{1}^{2}\sqrt{n/p}$ is dominated by the term $\sqrt{n/dp}$ since $\mu_{1}^{2}\leq\Tr\Sigma\lesssim d^{-1/2}$ , by (2.5). ∎

## 5. Proof of Proposition 4.3

We will compare $\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}$ with the clean data matrix $XX^{\mathsf{T}}$ through an intermediary. Let

$$ Y_{k}=\Pi^{(k)}_{Y}Y $$

denote the projection of the noisy data matrix $Y$ onto the subspace spanned by the eigenvectors corresponding to the largest $k$ eigenvalues of $YY^{\mathsf{T}}$ .

Proposition 4.3 follows immediately from the next two lemmas.

#### Lemma 5.1 (Clean data to projected noisy data).

With hypotheses as in Theorem 4.1, we have with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ that

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\mu_{1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}}. $$

#### Lemma 5.2 (Projected noisy data to embedding).

With hypotheses as in Theorem 4.1, we have that with probability $1-O(e^{-\sqrt{d}})$ that

$$ \|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,. $$

For the proofs of both lemmas we will use the following lemma showing that the top eigenvalues of $YY^{\mathsf{T}}$ concentrate near those of $XX^{\mathsf{T}}$ , up to a negligible shift.

#### Lemma 5.3.

With probability at least $1-e^{-d}$ ,

$$ \|Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y-(X^{\mathsf{T}}X+\tfrac{n}{d}I_{d})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}\,. $$

By Weyl’s inequality, on the same event we have

$$ \lambda_{i}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)=n\mu_{i}^{2}+\frac{n}{d}+O(\sqrt{n}\mu_{1})\qquad\forall 1\leq i\leq d $$

and in particular, by our assumptions $\mu_{1}^{2}\geq\mu_{k}^{2}=\omega(1/d)$ and $d<n$ ,

$$ \lambda_{1}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)=\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq(1+o(1))n\mu_{1}^{2}. $$

Moreover, with probability at least $1-e^{-\sqrt{d}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{i}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)\geq n\mu_{i}^{2}+\frac{n}{d}-O\left(\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}d^{-1/4}\right)\qquad\forall 1\leq i\leq k, \displaystyle\lambda_{k+1}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)\leq\frac{n}{d}+O\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}\right) $$

and consequently,

$$ \lambda_{k}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)-\lambda_{k+1}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)\geq(1-o(1))n\mu_{k}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

We start by proving (5.3). We have

$$ \displaystyle\Big\|Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y-(X^{\mathsf{T}}X+\frac{n}{d}I_{d})\Big\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\Big\|X^{\mathsf{T}}Z+Z^{\mathsf{T}}X+(Z^{\mathsf{T}}Z-\frac{n}{d}I_{d})\Big\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|X^{\mathsf{T}}Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\big\|Z^{\mathsf{T}}Z-\frac{n}{d}I_{d}\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,. $$

From [28, Theorem 4.6.1], we have

$$ \|Z^{\mathsf{T}}Z-\frac{n}{d}I_{d}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C\sqrt{n/d} $$

with probability at least $1-e^{-10d}$ , for a universal constant $C>0$ . Moreover, with $X=UDV^{\mathsf{T}}$ the singular value decomposition of $X$ , with $D,V$ of sizes $d\times d$ and $U$ having $d$ orthonormal columns in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , we have

$$ \|X^{\mathsf{T}}Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|DU^{\mathsf{T}}Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|U^{\mathsf{T}}Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}\|U^{\mathsf{T}}Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Now note that by rotational invariance of the distribution of the Gaussian columns of $Z$ , the $d\times d$ matrix $U^{\mathsf{T}}Z$ is identically distributed to a Gaussian matrix $G$ with independent centered entries of variance $1/d$ . Again from [28, Theorem 4.6.1] (or classical bounds) we thus have

$$ \|U^{\mathsf{T}}Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim 1 $$

with probability at least $1-e^{-10d}$ . By the union bound, (5.3) follows by substituting the above bound and (5.9) into (5.8). (Note that $\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}\geq\sqrt{n}\mu_{k}\geq\sqrt{n/d}$ by our assumption (2.7), so the first term in (5.8) dominates.)

Now we estimate $\lambda_{i}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)$ using (5.3) via Cauchy interlacing. First, recall the decomposition (6.1) and let $a_{i}=\bar{x}_{i}+N_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ , where $N_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{k}/d)$ are i.i.d. and $\bar{x}_{i}$ ’s are $x_{i}$ ’s with the last $d-k$ zeros removed. Let $\bar{Y}=\bar{X}+N\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ where the rows of $\bar{X}$ are $\bar{x}_{i}$ and the rows of $N$ are $N_{i}$ . Let $W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d-k}$ be formed by the last $d-k$ columns of $Y$ , so that $Y=(\bar{Y}\;W)$ . Notice that with this coordinate decomposition, one can write

$$ Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y=\begin{pmatrix}\bar{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{Y}&\bar{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}W\\
W^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{Y}&W^{\mathsf{T}}W\end{pmatrix} $$

Then, by the Cauchy Interlacing theorem, we can interlace the eigenvalues of $\lambda_{i}(YY^{T})=\lambda_{i}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)$ ( $1\leq i\leq d$ ) with those of $\lambda_{i}(\bar{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{Y})$ :

$$ \lambda_{i}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)\geq\lambda_{i}(\bar{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{Y}),\qquad\forall 1\leq i\leq k. $$

Now we repeat the proof of (5.3) but with $\bar{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{Y}$ in place of $Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y$ . Instead of (5.8) we have that

$$ \|\bar{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{Y}-(\bar{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{X}+\frac{n}{d}I_{k})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2\|\bar{X}^{\mathsf{T}}N\|+\|N^{\mathsf{T}}N-\frac{n}{d}I_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Similarly to the reduction (5.10), we use the truncated singular value decomposition of $X$ : $\bar{X}=U_{k}D_{k}V_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}$ where $U_{k},V_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ are the top $-k$ right and left singular vectors of $X$ (or equivalently, $\bar{X}$ ). Thus, by [28, Theorem 4.6.1] , with probability at least $1-\exp(-10d^{1/2})$ ,

$$ \|U_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}N\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\frac{2\sqrt{k}+O(d^{1/4})}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

This is due to the fact that $U_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}N$ is $k\times k$ . Moreover, analogously to (5.9), with probability $1-\exp(-10d^{1/2})$ ,

$$ \|N^{\mathsf{T}}N-\frac{n}{d}I_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{\sqrt{nk}+\sqrt{n}d^{1/4}+k+\sqrt{d}}{d}\lesssim\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}\frac{1}{d^{1/4}}, $$

where the last step uses $\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{k}=\omega(d^{-1/2})$ and $k=o(\sqrt{d}/\log^{2}n)$ by Remark 2.7. Now we apply the upper bounds from previous two displays to (5.13) to get that

$$ \|\bar{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{Y}-(\bar{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{X}+\frac{n}{d}I_{k})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}}{d^{1/4}}. $$

Now we combine (5.14) with Weyl’s inequality to estimate eigenvalues of $\bar{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\bar{Y}$ and thus the eigenvalues of $Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y$ via (5.12). Thus we obtain the first line of (5.6). To prove the second line of (5.6) we again use the Cauchy Interlacing Theorem, now with $\lambda_{k+1}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)\leq\lambda_{1}(W^{\mathsf{T}}W)$ . By [28, Theorem 4.4.5] with probability at least $1-e^{-d}$

$$ \lambda_{1}(W^{\mathsf{T}}W)=\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\leq\frac{(\sqrt{n}+2\sqrt{d})^{2}}{d}\leq\frac{n}{d}+C\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}. $$

Finally, (5.7) is proved using (5.6) with $i=k$ , and taking a difference:

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{k}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y)-\lambda_{k+1}(Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y) \displaystyle\geq n\mu_{k}^{2}+\frac{n}{d}-O(\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}d^{-1/4})+O\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{n}{d}}\right) \displaystyle=n\mu_{k}^{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{d\mu_{k}^{2}}+O\left(-\tfrac{\mu_{1}}{\sqrt{n}d^{1/4}\mu_{k}^{2}}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{nd}\mu_{k}^{2}}\right)\right). $$

(2.7) implies that the term $\frac{1}{d\mu_{k}^{2}}=o(1)$ . As for the error term, (2.5), (2.7) and $d<n$ imply that $\tfrac{\mu_{1}}{\sqrt{n}d^{1/4}\mu_{k}^{2}}\leq\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{dn\log n}\mu_{k}^{2}}=o(1)$ , $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{dn}\mu_{k}^{2}}=o(1)$ . ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 5.1.

By the triangle inequality and sub-multiplicativity of the operator norm,

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-XY_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|XY_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq(\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}})\|X-Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,. $$

Then, combining a triangle inequality and the fact that $Y_{k}$ is the best rank- $k$ approximation to $Y$ (the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem):

$$ \|X-Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|X-Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|Y-Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2\|X-Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

From (5.5) and (5.9) we have that with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ , $\|Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}=\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ and $\|X-Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\sqrt{n/d}$ . Substituting these bounds into (5.15) yields the claim. ∎

For the proof of Lemma 5.2 we use the following classical result (see e.g. [29, Theorem 2]):

#### Lemma 5.4 (Davis–Kahan inequality for spectral projections).

Consider two symmetric matrices A and B with spectral decompositions $A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}u_{i}u_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $B=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}v_{i}v_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}$ , in which the eigenvalues are (weakly) decreasing. Then the spectral projections $\Pi^{(k)}_{A}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}u_{i}u_{i}^{\mathsf{T}},\Pi^{(k)}_{B}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}v_{i}v_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}$ satisfy

$$ \|\Pi^{(k)}_{A}-\Pi^{(k)}_{B}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2\frac{\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{k+1}}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 5.2.

Recall that $\Pi^{(k)}_{M}$ denotes the projection matrix for the span of the top $k$ eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix $M$ . For brevity, in this part of the proof, we let $\Pi=\Pi^{(k)}_{Y}$ and $\hat{\Pi}=\Pi^{(k)}_{\hat{Y}}$ . Then we decompose $Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}$ using projections as follows:

$$ \displaystyle Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}} \displaystyle=\Pi YY^{\mathsf{T}}\Pi-\hat{\Pi}\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\hat{\Pi} \displaystyle=\underbrace{(\Pi YY^{\mathsf{T}}\Pi-\hat{\Pi}YY^{\mathsf{T}}\Pi)}_{(i)}+\underbrace{(\hat{\Pi}YY^{\mathsf{T}}\Pi-\hat{\Pi}YY^{\mathsf{T}}\hat{\Pi})}_{(ii)}+\underbrace{(\hat{\Pi}YY^{\mathsf{T}}\hat{\Pi}-\hat{\Pi}\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\hat{\Pi})\,.}_{(iii)} $$

We dedicate the rest of the proof to estimating the operator norms of $(i)-(iii)$ :

- $(i+ii)$ By sub-multiplicativity of the operator norm and Lemma 5.4, $\displaystyle\|\Pi YY^{\mathsf{T}}\Pi-\hat{\Pi}YY^{\mathsf{T}}\Pi\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ $\displaystyle\leq\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}\Pi\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\Pi-\hat{\Pi}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ $\displaystyle\leq 2\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\frac{\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})}.$ By similar lines we obtain the same bound for $(ii)$ .

- (iii) By sub-multiplicativity of the operator norm: $\displaystyle\|\hat{\Pi}YY^{\mathsf{T}}\hat{\Pi}-\hat{\Pi}\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\hat{\Pi}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ $\displaystyle\leq\|\hat{\Pi}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}.$

Combining the bounds for $(i)$ – $(iii)$ with (5.16) and the triangle inequality yields

$$ \|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\left(\frac{\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})}+1\right)\asymp\frac{\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})} $$

Finally, from Lemma 5.3 we have $\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq(1+o(1))n\mu_{1}^{2}$ and $\lambda_{k}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\geq(1-o(1))n\mu_{k}^{2}$ with probability $1-O(e^{-\sqrt{d}})$ . Substituting these estimates in the above display yields the claim. ∎

## 6. Proof of Proposition 4.4

### 6.1. Setup and overview

We broadly follow the approach of [21], expressing the entries of $A$ as functions of inner products of unit vectors and expanding in the basis of Gegenbauer polynomials. Since the distribution of the Gaussian matrix $Z$ is invariant under multiplication on the left by fixed orthogonal matrices, and the SNGM construction only depends on the inner products, we may assume without loss of generality that the subspace spanned by rows of $X$ aligns with the first $k$ canonical coordinates. Thus, we write

$$ y_{i}=(a_{i},w_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\qquad a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k},\qquad w_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d-k}), $$

where $a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ contains the coordinates of $x_{i}$ plus the first $k$ coordinates of the noise, and $w_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d-k})$ represents the orthogonal noise component. We further decompose the Gaussian noise vector $w_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-k}$ into a magnitude $l_{i}=\|w_{i}\|_{2}$ and direction $v_{i}=\frac{w_{i}}{\|w_{i}\|_{2}}$ , thus

$$ y_{i}=(a_{i},l_{i}v_{i})\,. $$

Note that $a_{i},l_{i}$ and $v_{i}$ are jointly independent. For each $i\neq j\in[n]$ , the $(i,j)$ -th entry of the adjacency matrix is thus given by

$$ A_{ij}=\1(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau)=\1(\left\langle a_{i},a_{j}\right\rangle+l_{i}l_{j}\left\langle v_{i},v_{j}\right\rangle\geq\tau)=\1\left(\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{ij}\right), $$

where we define the (random) thresholds

$$ \tau^{ij}:=\frac{\tau-\left\langle a_{i},a_{j}\right\rangle}{l_{i}l_{j}}. $$

In Lemma 6.4 we show that $\tau^{ij}$ are concentrated around $\tau$ . Set

$$ \varphi(x):=\1(x\geq\sqrt{d-k}\tau)\,,\qquad\varphi_{ij}(x):=\1(x\geq\sqrt{d-k}\tau^{ij})\,. $$

We expand these functions in the basis of Gegenbauer polynomials $(q^{(d-k)}_{\ell})_{\ell\geq 0}$ . Recall that $(q^{(m)}_{\ell})_{\ell\geq 0}$ is an orthogonal basis for $L^{2}([-\sqrt{m},\sqrt{m}],\mathcal{D}_{m})$ , where $\mathcal{D}_{m}$ denotes the distribution of $\sqrt{m}\langle u_{1},u_{2}\rangle$ for independent uniformly drawn elements of the unit sphere $\mathcal{S}^{m-1}$ (thus, $\mathcal{D}_{m}$ is the distribution of any fixed entry of $\sqrt{m}u_{1}$ ). The first three are given by

$$ q_{0}^{(m)}(x)=1\,,\qquad q_{1}^{(m)}(x)=x\,,\qquad q_{2}^{(m)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{\frac{m+2}{m-1}}(x^{2}-1)\,. $$

We define expansion coefficients $p_{\ell},p^{ij}_{\ell}$ with

$$ \varphi(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sqrt{N_{\ell}^{(d-k)}}p_{\ell}q_{\ell}^{(d-k)}(x)\,,\qquad\varphi_{ij}(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sqrt{N_{\ell}^{(d-k)}}p^{ij}_{\ell}q_{\ell}^{(d-k)}(x) $$

where we have scaled the degree- $\ell$ parts by the square-roots of integers

$$ N_{0}^{(m)}=1\,,\qquad N_{\ell}^{(m)}=\frac{2\ell+m-2}{\ell}\binom{\ell+m-3}{\ell-1}\,,\quad\ell\geq 1, $$

giving the cardinality of the orthonormal degree- $\ell$ spherical harmonics on $\mathcal{S}^{m-1}$ . (Note that for the case $\ell=1$ the above definition for $p_{1}$ agrees with our earlier definition (4.4).) For a review of spherical harmonics and Gegenbauer polynomials see for instance [18, 6, 12].

The orthogonal expansion (6.6) of $\varphi_{ij}$ induces an expansion

$$ A=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}A^{(\ell)}\,,\qquad\text{where}\quad A^{(\ell)}_{ij}=\sqrt{N_{\ell}^{(d-k)}}p^{ij}_{\ell}q_{\ell}^{(d-k)}(\sqrt{d-k}\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle)\,. $$

In particular,

$$ A^{(0)}=P_{0}\,,\qquad A^{(1)}=(d-k)P_{1}\odot(VV^{\mathsf{T}}) $$

where $V^{\mathsf{T}}=(v_{1}^{\mathsf{T}},\dots,v_{n}^{\mathsf{T}})$ ,

$$ P_{\ell}:=(p_{\ell}^{ij}1_{i\neq j})_{i,j=1}^{n} $$

and we recall our notation $\odot$ for the entrywise product of matrices. We use the Gegenbauer expansion (6.8) of the adjacency matrix $A$ to bridge the gap between $YY^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ .

#### Definition 6.1 (Data, spherical and spectral approximations).

We set

$$ \boxed{\begin{aligned} B_{\text{data}}&:=p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}+d_{k}p_{1}YY^{\mathsf{T}},\\
B_{\text{sph}}&:=P_{0}+d_{k}P_{1}\odot(VV^{\mathsf{T}})\\
B_{\text{spec}}&:=\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}+d_{k}p_{1}\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\end{aligned}} $$

where $\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ has entries

$$ \zeta_{i}:=1+\frac{(l_{i}-1)p_{1}d_{k}\tau}{p_{0}} $$

Here and in the sequel we write

$$ d_{k}:=d-k\,. $$

Recalling (6.9), we see that $B_{\text{sph}}=A^{(0)}+A^{(1)}$ collects the order 0 and 1 terms of the Gegenbauer expansion of $A$ .

For the proof of Proposition 4.4 we note that

$$ \displaystyle d_{k}p_{1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}) \displaystyle=B_{\text{data}}-B_{\text{spec}}+\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}} \displaystyle=(B_{\text{data}}-A)+(A-B_{\text{spec}})+(\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}). $$

Since $B_{\text{spec}}$ is the best rank- $(d+1)$ approximation to $A$ under the operator norm, and $B_{\text{data}}$ has rank at most $d+1$ , we may thus bound

$$ \displaystyle d_{k}p_{1}\|\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-YY^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|B_{\text{spec}}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|A-B_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|A-B_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|A-B_{\text{sph}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|B_{\text{sph}}-B_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} $$

The three terms in the final line are bounded in Lemmas 6.10, 6.11 and 6.14.

### 6.3. Spherical to Data Error

In the following division of this section, we will focus on controlling the spherical to data error component $\|B_{\text{sph}}-B_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . The proof is split into different regimes according to the size of the trace.

#### Lemma 6.11 (Data Matrix is well approximated by Spherical Component).

Under the conditions as Theorem 4.1, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-12})$ :

$$ \big\lVert B_{\text{sph}}-B_{\text{data}}\big\rVert_{op}\lesssim np\big(\tau^{2}+d\mu_{1}^{2}(\Tr\Sigma)\big)\log^{4}(n). $$

In the proof of Lemma 6.11 we make frequent use of the following:

#### Fact 6.12 (Infinity norm bound).

$$ \|M\|_{op}\leq\|M\|_{F}\leq n\|M\|_{\infty} $$

for an $n\times n$ matrix $M$ , where $\|M\|_{\infty}:=\max_{i,j}|M_{ij}|$ .

#### Fact 6.13 (Hadamard Product Bound [19, 7.5.P24]).

If $A$ is positive semi-definite, then

$$ \|A\odot B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|A\|_{\infty}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 6.11.

We want an upper bound on the operator norm of the matrix

$$ \diag(B_{\text{sph}})_{ii}:=p_{0}^{ii}-d_{k}p_{1}^{ii}\|v_{i}\|_{2}^{2}. $$

$$ \|\diag(B_{\text{sph}})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim O(p\sqrt{d\log n}), $$

with probability at least $1-O(n^{-12})$ . (6.22) is much smaller than the resulting error we are looking for (see the theorem statement Lemma 6.11). We call the matrices that include $p^{ii}_{0},p_{1}^{ii}$ on their diagonals $P_{0}^{\diag},P_{1}^{\diag}$ respectively.

Since $aa^{\mathsf{T}}\odot(\1L^{\mathsf{T}}+L\1^{\mathsf{T}})=aa^{\mathsf{T}}\diag(L)+\diag(L)aa^{\mathsf{T}}$ , and using part (c) of Lemma 6.9 to control $\|\Delta\tau^{\odot 2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ , and $\|aa^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\mu_{1}^{2}$ , $\|\diag(L)\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\sqrt{\log n/d})$ , $\displaystyle\|f_{1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ $\displaystyle\lesssim p_{1}d_{k}\Big[\|aa^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\diag(L)\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\tfrac{n\tau\log n}{d}\Big]+O(pd^{2}\tau^{2})\,\|\Delta\tau^{\odot 2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ $\displaystyle\lesssim np\tau\sqrt{d}\,\mu_{1}^{2}\log^{1/2}n+np\tau^{2}\log n+npd^{2}\tau^{2}\bigg(\mu_{1}^{2}\,\Tr\Sigma\log n+\frac{\tau^{2}\log^{3}n}{d}\bigg),$ where we used $d^{2}\tau^{2}=dO(\log n)$ . $$ \boxed{\ \|f_{1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim np\big(\tau^{2}+d\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr\Sigma\big)\log^{4}n,\ } $$

on the same event as Lemma 6.8 and Lemma 6.9, which both occur with probability at least $1-O(n^{-12})$ . which probability at least $1-O(n^{-12})$ (since (6.22) also occurs with at least probability $1-O(n^{-12})$ as with all the $f_{1},\dots,f_{4}$ ) which concludes the proof. ∎

### 6.4. Rank-1 difference

This section establishes the following bound for the third term in (6.14).

#### Lemma 6.14.

Under the conditions of Theorem 4.1, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim npd\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma)\log^{4}(n)+\max\{np\tau^{2},\sqrt{np}\}\log^{9}n+dp\tau\log^{4}n. $$

Recall that the overall goal of Proposition 4.4 is to control $\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . The first term $YY^{\mathsf{T}}$ is contained in $B_{\text{data}}$ , while the other, is contained in the spectral decomposition of $A$ (which we called $B_{\text{spec}}$ ). $B_{\text{spec}}$ is expressed in terms of orthogonal eigenvectors of $A$ , however, for the components of $B_{\text{data}}=p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}+d_{k}p_{1}YY^{\mathsf{T}}$ , we don’t necessarily know that $\zeta$ and $Y$ lie in orthogonal vector spaces, so we must force orthogonality. Consequently, the strategy for this part of the proof will be to project $YY^{\mathsf{T}}$ away from the subspace spanned by $\zeta$ . Then we use Davis–Kahan to compare $\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}$ .

#### Lemma 6.15.

Under the same conditions as Theorem 4.1, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}\|_{op}=O(\log^{4}n) $$

where we denote the projection $\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}=I-\frac{\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}}{\lVert\zeta\rVert_{2}^{2}}$ .

#### Proof.

We have

$$ YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}=-\frac{\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}}{\lVert\zeta\rVert^{2}}YY^{\mathsf{T}}-YY^{\mathsf{T}}\frac{\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}}{\lVert\zeta\rVert^{2}}+\frac{\lVert\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y\rVert^{2}}{\lVert\zeta\rVert^{4}}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}. $$

We use concentration to estimate the norm $\lVert\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y\rVert_{2}^{2}$ , first when $|(\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y)_{j}|$ where $j\leq k$ , we note that $z_{ij}$ is independent from $\|w_{i}\|_{2}-1=l_{i}-1$ (here, it is useful to visualize the decomposition $z_{i}=(N_{i},w_{i})$ from the proof of (5.6)), so the term $L_{i}\frac{p_{1}d_{k}\tau}{p_{0}}=O\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{\log n}{d}}\Big)\cdot O(\log n)=O\Big(\tfrac{\log^{3/2}n}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)=o(1),$ with high probability. Therefore, by using Gaussian concentration, with probability at least $1-n^{-10}$ we have that for all $j\leq k$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|(\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y)_{j}| \displaystyle=\Bigg|\sum^{n}_{i=1}(1+L_{i}\ p_{1}d_{k}\tau/p_{0})(x_{ij}+z_{ij})\Bigg| \displaystyle\lesssim(1+\log n\sqrt{d}\tau^{2})\sqrt{n\log n(\tfrac{1}{d}+\Tr\left(\Sigma\right))} \displaystyle\lesssim\sqrt{n\log n(\tfrac{1}{d}+\Tr\left(\Sigma\right))}\,. $$

For $j>k$ ,

$$ |(\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y)_{j}|=\Bigg|\sum^{n}_{i=1}(1+L_{i}\ p_{1}d_{k}\tau/p_{0})z_{ij}\Bigg|\leq\Bigg|\sum^{n}_{i=1}z_{ij}\Bigg|+p_{1}d_{k}\tau/p_{0}\Bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}(l_{i}-1)z_{ij}\Bigg|. $$

By Gaussian concentration, the first term is of order $O(\sqrt{n\log n/d})$ . To control the second term, we first condition on the event $\mathcal{L}=\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\{L_{i}\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}\}$ and note that $z_{ij}=l_{i}v_{ij}$ . Thus, applying Hoeffding’s inequality for bounded random variables (e.g. see [28, Theorem 2.2.6]) to $v_{ij}$ , which are independent for different $i$ given a fixed $j$ and centered, we get that

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{i}(l_{i}-1)v_{ij}\right|\geq t\big|\mathcal{L}\right)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{L})\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{ct^{2}d_{k}}{O(n\log(n)/d)}\right). $$

On the right hand side, we used the bound $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{L})\leq 1$ and the fact that on the event $\mathcal{L}$ , each summand satisfies $l_{i}^{2}(l_{i}-1)^{2}=l_{i}^{2}L_{i}^{2}=O(\log n/d)$ deterministically, since $l_{i}=1+L_{i}=1+O(\sqrt{\log n/d})$ on $\mathcal{L}$ , so summing over $n$ gives $O(n\log(n)/d)$ . Undoing the conditioning on $\mathcal{L}$ , we then have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{i}(l_{i}-1)v_{ij}\right|\geq t\right) \displaystyle\quad\leq\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{L})\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{i}(l_{i}-1)v_{ij}\right|\geq t\big|\mathcal{L}\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{L}^{c}\right)\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{i}(l_{i}-1)v_{ij}\right|\geq t\big|\mathcal{L}^{c}\right) \displaystyle\quad\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{i}(l_{i}-1)v_{ij}\right|\geq t\big|\mathcal{L}\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{L}^{c}\right)\quad\text{ by }\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{L}),\mathbb{P}\left(\sum l_{i}(l_{i}-1)v_{ij}|\mathcal{L}^{c}\right)\leq 1 \displaystyle\quad\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{ct^{2}d_{k}}{O(n\log n/d)}\right)+n^{-12}\qquad\text{by \lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{lemma:ai_aj_li_lj_conc}}. $$

Finally, setting $t=C\frac{\sqrt{n}}{d}\log n$ for sufficiently large $C$ we get that with probability at least $1-n^{-12}$

$$ \bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{i}(l_{i}-1)v_{ij}\bigg|=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}\log n}{d}\right). $$

Once again, the first term in the expression for $(\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y)_{j}$ is the dominant one, so

$$ (\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y)_{j}\lesssim\sqrt{n\log n/d}\qquad j>k. $$

Taking the norm, and a union bound over the probabilities, we obtain that with probability at least $1-dn^{-12}\geq 1-n^{-10}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lVert\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y\rVert_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=kO\left({n\log n(\tfrac{1}{d}+\Tr\left(\Sigma\right))}\right)+(d-k)O\left(\frac{n\log^{4}n}{d}\right)=O(n\log^{4}n). $$

Since $\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)=O(1)$ , with probability at least $1-n^{-10}$

$$ \displaystyle\lVert\frac{\lVert\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y\rVert^{2}}{\lVert\zeta\rVert^{4}}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\frac{\lVert\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y\rVert^{2}}{\lVert\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\rVert^{2}}=O(\log^{4}n). $$

Similarly, with probability at least $1-n^{-10}$

$$ \big\lVert\frac{\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}}{\|\zeta\|^{2}_{2}}YY^{\mathsf{T}}\big\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{d}\big\lVert\frac{(\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}Y)_{j}^{2}}{\|\zeta\|^{2}_{2}}\big\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\log^{4}n). $$

This concludes the proof of Lemma 6.15. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 6.14.

We would like to apply Davis–Kahan to Lemma 6.15, so we need to find the spectral gap of

$$ B_{\text{proj}}:=p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}+d_{k}p_{1}\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}. $$

To this end, following Equation 5.3 the first eigenvalue of the matrix $B_{\text{proj}}$ can be estimated with Lemma 6.4, which tells us that $|\zeta_{i}|=O(1+\sqrt{\log n/d}\tau^{2}d)$ , thus;

$$ \lambda_{1}(B_{\text{proj}})=\Theta(pn), $$

while the second eigenvalue

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{2}(B_{\text{proj}}) \displaystyle=d_{k}p_{1}\lambda_{1}(\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}) \displaystyle\leq d_{k}p_{1}\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}\|^{2}_{\mathrm{op}}\quad\text{by sub-multiplicativity} \displaystyle\leq d_{k}p_{1}O\left(n\mu_{1}^{2}+\frac{n}{d}+O\left(\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}\right)\right)\quad\text{ by }\lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{lem:eval_conc} \displaystyle\leq dp\sqrt{\tfrac{\log n}{d}}O\big(\tfrac{n}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}\big) \displaystyle=o(pn). $$

Therefore, by the Davis–Kahan theorem, there exists $\theta\in\{-1,1\}$ such that

$$ \|\theta\mathbf{w}_{0}-\frac{\zeta}{\|\zeta\|_{2}}\|_{2}\lesssim\frac{\|A-B_{\text{proj}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{1}(B_{\text{proj}})-\lambda_{2}(B_{\text{proj}})} $$

From the triangle inequality and Lemmas 6.15, 6.10 and 6.11,

$$ \displaystyle\|A-B_{\text{proj}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\|A-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}-d_{k}p_{1}\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq d_{k}p_{1}\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\Pi^{\perp}_{\zeta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|A-B_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim dp\tau\log^{4}(n)+npd\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma)\log^{2}(n)+\max\{np\tau^{2},\sqrt{np}\}\log^{9}n \displaystyle\lesssim npd\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma)\log^{2}(n)+\max\{np\tau^{2},\sqrt{np}\}\log^{9}n+dp\tau\log^{4}n. $$

The last inequality was obtained by taking dominant terms. Now assume without loss of generality that $\theta=1$ in (6.31). Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq|\eta_{0}-p_{0}\|\zeta\|_{2}^{2}|+p_{0}\|\zeta\|_{2}^{2}\|\mathbf{w}_{0}-\frac{\zeta}{\|\zeta\|}_{2}\|_{2} \displaystyle\leq\underbrace{\|A-B_{\text{proj}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}_{\text{by Weyl's inequality}}+\underbrace{\Theta(pn)}_{=\lambda_{1}(B_{\text{proj}})}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\|A-B_{\text{proj}}\|}{\Theta(pn)-o(pn)}}_{\text{by }\ref{eqn:DavisKahanEigenVectors}\text{ and }\ref{eqn:lambd2a_Bprj}} \displaystyle\leq\Theta(1)\left(npd\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma)\log^{4}(n)+\max\{np\tau^{2},\sqrt{np}\}\log^{9}n\right)+dp\tau\log^{4}n $$

which completes the proof. ∎

### 6.5. Proof of Proposition 4.4

Inserting the bounds from Lemmas 6.10, 6.11 and 6.14 into (6.14), we have

$$ \displaystyle\|d_{k}p_{1}YY^{\mathsf{T}}-d_{k}p_{1}\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq(\text{Adjacency to Spherical})+(\text{Spherical to Data})+(\text{Rank-1 difference}) \displaystyle\lesssim npd(\tau^{2}+\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma))\log^{4}(n)+\max\{np\tau^{2},\sqrt{np}\}\log^{9}n+dp\tau\log^{4}n. $$

From Lemma 6.4 we have $p_{1}=\Theta(p\tau)$ , so we may divide through by $d_{k}p_{1}\asymp dp\tau$ to obtain

$$ \|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\sqrt{d}\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma)\log^{4}(n)+\left(n\frac{\tau}{d}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}\right)\log^{9}n+\log^{4}n. $$

Noticing that $\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}\log^{9}(n)\geq\log^{4}n$ and $np\tau^{2}\log^{9}n\geq np\tau^{2}\log^{4}n$ , gives the statement of the Proposition.∎

## 7. Generalization to Numerically Low-Rank Data

In this section we prove Theorem 2.5, which relaxes the strict rank assumption of Theorem 4.1. The general approach is to pass to a low-rank projection of the data matrix $X$ . Hence, the statements and proofs of many lemmas and propositions mirror those of Theorem 4.1, but additional arguments are needed to handle errors arising from the spectral projection.

Recall our notation $\Pi^{(k)}_{M}$ for the matrix for projection to the span of the top $k$ eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix $M$ . Write $X_{k}:=\Pi^{(k)}_{X}X$ , and set

#### Lemma 7.1.

With probability at least $1-e^{-\sqrt{d}}$ , $\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\leq\frac{n}{d}+O\Big(\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}+\frac{n\mu_{k+1}}{\sqrt{d}}+n\mu_{k+1}^{2}\Big)$ . The estimates of $\lambda_{i}(YY^{\mathsf{T}}),1\leq i\leq k$ agree with Lemma 5.3.

#### Lemma 7.2 (Clean Data and Noisy Data Projection Matrix Distance Generalized).

Under the same conditions as Theorem 2.5, with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ ,

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\mu_{1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is analogous to Lemma 5.1, except for the first triangle inequality which separates the trailing eigenvalues of $XX^{\mathsf{T}}$ from the first $k$ .

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|X_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+(\|X_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}})\|X_{k}-Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,. $$

The first term on the right hand side of (7.3) is $n\mu_{k+1}^{2}$ . For the second summand on the right hand side, we have that with probability at least $1-e^{-d}$ ,

$$ \|X_{k}-Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2\|X_{k}-Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=2\|X_{k}-(X+Z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2(\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}+\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}})\lesssim\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}. $$

Then, combining (7.3) and (7.4) with bounds from the proof of Lemma 5.1 yields

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\mu_{k+1}^{2}+n\mu_{1}(\mu_{k+1}+1/\sqrt{d}). $$

From the conditions (2.7) it follows $\mu_{k+1}\leq d^{-1/2}\leq\mu_{k}\leq\mu_{1}$ , so the right hand side is $O(n\mu_{1}/\sqrt{d})$ as claimed. ∎

#### Lemma 7.3 (Original and Truncated Data Difference).

Under the same conditions as Theorem 2.5, we have with probability at least $1-e^{-\sqrt{d}}$ ,

$$ \|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\mu_{k+1}. $$

#### Proof.

Recall that $\tilde{Y}_{k}=\Pi_{\tilde{Y}}^{(k)}(X_{k}+Z),Y_{k}=\Pi_{Y}^{(k)}(X+Z)$ , for short, we will use $\Pi=\Pi^{(k)}_{Y}$ as in the proof of Lemma 5.2 and $\tilde{\Pi}=\Pi^{(k)}_{\tilde{Y}}$ Using the triangle inequality, we introduce an intermediate term $\Pi^{(k)}_{Y}\tilde{Y}=\Pi\tilde{Y}$ :

$$ \|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\Pi\tilde{Y}(\Pi\tilde{Y})^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\Pi\tilde{Y}(\Pi\tilde{Y})^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} $$

Then, estimating the first term on the right hand side via concentration of the operator norm of $Z$ (e.g. [28, Theorem 4.4.5]) yields, that with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\Pi\tilde{Y}(\Pi\tilde{Y})^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\left\|\Pi\left[X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-XX^{\mathsf{T}}+(X_{k}-X)Z^{\mathsf{T}}+Z(X_{k}-X)^{\mathsf{T}}\right]\Pi\right\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-XX^{\mathsf{T}}+(X_{k}-X)Z^{\mathsf{T}}+Z(X_{k}-X)^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|X-X_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=n\mu_{k+1}^{2}+2\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim n\mu_{k+1}^{2}+n\mu_{k+1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\mu_{k+1} $$

where we used (5.9) in the final line. As for the second expression in (7.6), we write

$$ \displaystyle\|\Pi\tilde{Y}(\Pi\tilde{Y})^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\|(\Pi-\tilde{\Pi})\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\tilde{\Pi}+\Pi\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}(\Pi-\tilde{\Pi})\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|\Pi-\tilde{\Pi}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\frac{\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})}\quad\text{ by \lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{DavisKahanForProjections}}. $$

By definition of $\tilde{Y}$ , we know that $\lambda_{1}(X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}})=n\mu_{1}^{2}=\lambda_{1}(XX^{\mathsf{T}})$ , so by the same argument as Lemma 5.3, $\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=n\mu_{1}^{2}+O(n/d)\lesssim n\mu_{1}^{2},$ with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ , and similarly combining Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 7.1 gives us an estimate on the eigenvalue gap

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{k}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}}) \displaystyle\geq n\mu_{k}^{2}+\frac{n}{d}-O\left(\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}d^{-1/4}\right)-\bigg(\frac{n}{d}+O\Big(\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}+\frac{n\mu_{k+1}}{\sqrt{d}}+n\mu_{k+1}^{2}\Big)\bigg) \displaystyle\gtrsim n\mu_{k}^{2}. $$

In the last line, we use (2.7), (2.5) and $d<n$ to obtain the dominant term. Then, by the same lines as in (7.7), we have that with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim n\mu_{k+1}/\sqrt{d}\,. $$

Plugging these estimates into (7.8), then adding to (7.7) gives us:

$$ \|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\mu_{k+1}+n\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}(\mu_{k+1}^{2}+\mu_{k+1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}})\lesssim\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\frac{n\mu_{k+1}}{\sqrt{d}}, $$

as claimed. ∎
