### 7.2. Comparison Step

Recall that in the proof of Theorem 2.5, we used Proposition 7.5, a quantitative control on $\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . In this subsection we explain how Proposition 7.5 follows from combining the arguments of Section 6 (replacing occurrences of $Y$ with $\tilde{Y}$ ) with a good enough quantitative bound on $\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ (see Proposition 7.6).

#### 7.2.1. Truncating the Adjacency Matrix

In this section, we will show that the observed adjacency matrix $A_{ij}=\1\left(y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)$ is well-approximated by adjacency matrix $\tilde{A}=\1\left(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)$ , induced by the strictly low-rank data. This is the first component that we need to find to prove Proposition 7.5.

#### Proposition 7.6 (Truncation Error).

Under the same assumptions as Theorem 2.5, and $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}>0$ (otherwise we reduce to the strictly rank $-k$ case, as we have already done in Theorem 4.1). Then, with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ :

$$ \|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\left(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\right)^{1/4}+\log n. $$

To prove this proposition, we first define a continuous approximation to the indicator function. For $\delta>0$ , let:

$$ I_{\delta}(x)=\begin{cases}0\quad&\text{ if }x<\tau-\delta,\\
\frac{1}{\delta}(x-\tau+\delta)\quad&\text{ if }\tau-\delta\leq x<\tau,\\
1\quad&\text{ if }x\geq\tau.\end{cases} $$

Note that $I_{\delta}$ is $(1/\delta)$ -Lipschitz and bounded between 0 and 1. Let $A_{\delta},\tilde{A}_{\delta}$ be matrices with entries $I_{\delta}(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle)$ , $I_{\delta}(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle)$ , respectively, where we recall that $\tilde{y}_{i}=\Pi^{(k)}_{X}x_{i}+z_{i}$ . We split the error as follows:

$$ \|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|A-A_{\delta}+\tilde{A}_{\delta}-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

#### Lemma 7.7 (Lipschitz Approximation Error).

Under the same conditions as Theorem 2.5, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ :

$$ \|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\delta\sqrt{d}}(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/2}\qquad\forall\delta>0. $$

#### Proof.

We will use the Frobenius norm to control the operator norm since $\|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{F}$ . Then, explicitly writing out the component-wise difference, we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle|I_{\delta}(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle)-I_{\delta}(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle)| \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\delta}|\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle-\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle|=:\frac{1}{\delta}M_{ij}, $$

and thus $\|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{F}\leq\frac{1}{\delta}\|M\|_{F}$ . We can express the matrix $M$ as a function of the noise vectors $M=M(Z)=\frac{1}{\delta}\left(X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}+X_{k+1:d}Z^{\mathsf{T}}+ZX_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\right)$ , where $Z$ contains the noise vectors as rows and $X_{k+1:d}=X-X_{k}=(I-\Pi^{(k)}_{X})X$ is the projection onto the tail eigenspace.

Note that for different inputs $W,W^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ , the reverse triangle inequality and the non-commutative Hölder inequality yield:

$$ \displaystyle\big|\|M(W)\|_{F}-\|M(W^{\prime})\|_{F}\big| \displaystyle\leq\|M(W)-M(W^{\prime})\|_{F} \displaystyle=\|X_{k+1:d}(W-W^{\prime})^{\mathsf{T}}+(W-W^{\prime})X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq 2\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}\|W-W^{\prime}\|_{F}. $$

Therefore $\|M(Z)\|_{F}$ is a $2\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}$ -Lipschitz function (with respect to the Euclidean Frobenius metric) of Gaussian noise with variance $\frac{1}{d}$ . From Gaussian concentration (see [28, Theorem 5.2.3 ]) it follows

$$ \mathbb{P}(\|M\|_{F}-\mathbb{E}\|M\|_{F}\geq t)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{ct^{2}d}{n\mu^{2}_{k+1}}\right) $$

for any $t>0$ . Moreover, it is straightforward to control the expectation:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|M\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}+2\mathbb{E}\|X_{k+1:d}Z^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\bigg(\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}+2\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}\bigg)\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F} \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\sqrt{\sum_{l>k}\mu_{l}^{2}}. $$

The lemma follows by setting $t=C\sqrt{n/d}\mu_{k+1}\log n$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$ , and noting that $\mu_{k+1}\log n\leq\sqrt{n\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}}$ . ∎

Now, we want to control the other part of the triangle inequality in (7.12), which captures the discontinuity of the hard indicator. Let $g(x)=\1(x\geq\tau)-I_{\delta}(x)$ , $Q_{ij}=\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle$ , and $\tilde{Q}_{ij}=\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle$ . Let $H$ be the symmetric matrix with entries $(A-A_{\delta}+\tilde{A}_{\delta}-\tilde{A})_{ij}=g(Q_{ij})-g(\tilde{Q}_{ij})$ . By the Schur test,

$$ \|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|H_{ij}| $$

Note that $0\leq|g(x)|\leq\1(x\in[\tau-\delta,\tau])$ . Thus, with $D_{ij}:=\1(Q_{ij}\in[\tau-\delta,\tau])$ and $\tilde{D}_{ij}:=\1(\tilde{Q}_{ij}\in[\tau-\delta,\tau])$ , we have

$$ |H_{ij}|\leq 2(D_{ij}+\tilde{D}_{ij})\qquad\forall i,j\in[n]. $$

#### Claim 7.8.

For any $\delta>0$ , with probability $1-O(e^{-cd})+O(ne^{-c\delta\sqrt{d}n})$ ,

$$ \max_{1\leq i\leq n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{ij}\lesssim\delta\sqrt{d}n\,. $$

The same holds with $\tilde{D}$ in place of $D$ .

We first conclude the proof of Proposition 7.6 on the claim.

#### Proof of Proposition 7.6.

Let $\delta>0$ to be chosen. From (7.12), Lemma 7.7, (7.17) and Claim 7.8,

$$ \|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\delta\sqrt{d}}(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/2}+\delta\sqrt{d}n $$

with probability $1-O(n^{-10}+e^{-cd}+e^{-c\delta\sqrt{d}n})$ . Taking $\delta=d^{-1/2}(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/4}+C\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{d}n}$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$ concludes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Claim 7.8.

We only give the argument for $D$ ; the argument for $\tilde{D}$ being almost identical.

Fixing an arbitrary $i\in[n]$ , note that conditional on $z_{i}$ , the $n-1$ variables $(Q_{ij})_{j\neq i}$ are independent and Gaussian, with $Q_{ij}$ having mean $\langle y_{i},x_{j}\rangle$ and variance $\|y_{i}\|_{2}^{2}/d$ . In particular, the conditional density of $Q_{ij}$ given $z_{i}$ is bounded by $O(\sqrt{d}/\|y_{i}\|_{2})$ . Letting $\mathcal{E}_{i}=\{\|y_{i}\|_{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}\}$ , we have that on $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ the variables $(D_{ij})_{j\neq i}$ are independent Bernoulli variables with expectations $O(\delta\sqrt{d})$ . From Bernstein’s inequality it follows $\1(\mathcal{E}_{i})\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{ij}\lesssim\delta\sqrt{d}n$ with probability $1-O(\exp(-c\delta\sqrt{d}n))$ . Furthermore, we have $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{i})\geq 1-e^{-cd}$ for all $i\in[n]$ . Indeed, from (2.6) we have $\|x_{i}\|_{2}\lesssim\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma}=o(1)$ , while with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ , $\|z_{i}\|_{2}\in[\frac{1}{2},2]$ , and hence $\|y_{i}\|_{2}\geq\|z_{i}\|_{2}-\|x_{i}\|_{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}-o(1)$ . By the union bound, for $C$ sufficiently large we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{ij}>C\delta\sqrt{d}n\bigg) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{i}^{c})+\mathbb{P}\bigg(\1(\mathcal{E}_{i})\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{ij}>C\delta\sqrt{d}n\bigg) \displaystyle\lesssim n(e^{-cd}+e^{-c\delta\sqrt{d}n}) \displaystyle\lesssim e^{-cd}+ne^{-c\delta\sqrt{d}n} $$

where in the last bound we used that $d=\omega(\log n)$ . ∎

In some of the parameter estimates for the truncated case we will approximate $p$ with $\tilde{p}$ , which we justify below.

#### 7.2.2. Estimation for Truncated Parameters

In this part of the subsection, we show that there is asymptotically (up to leading order) no difference between the parameters of $A$ and $\tilde{A}$ . We begin with $\tilde{p}$ :

#### Lemma 7.9.

Under the same conditions as Proposition 7.6, we have that

$$ (1+o(1))p=\tilde{p}. $$

#### Proof.

We use the same notation as in the proof of Proposition 7.6. We will use that for any $s>0$ ,

$$ |\1(Q_{ij}\geq\tau)-\1(\tilde{Q}_{ij}\geq\tau)|\leq\1[|Q_{ij}-\tilde{Q}_{ij}|\geq s]+\1[|Q_{ij}-\tau|<s]+\1[|\tilde{Q}_{ij}-\tau|<s]\,. $$

Fixing $s>0$ to be optimized later, we have

$$ \displaystyle|p-\tilde{p}| \displaystyle=\bigg|\binom{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{P}\left(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)-\mathbb{P}\left(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)\bigg| \displaystyle\leq\binom{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{E}\big|\1\left(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)-\1\left(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)\big| \displaystyle\leq\binom{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{P}(|Q_{ij}-\tau|\leq s)+\mathbb{P}(|Q_{ij}-\tilde{Q}_{ij}|\geq s)+\mathbb{P}(|\tilde{Q}_{ij}-\tau|<s)\qquad\text{by }\eqref{eqn: entrywise_p_tildep_UB}. $$

All that is left is to estimate the probabilities on the right hand side above. Recall from the proof of Claim 7.8 that

$$ \mathbb{P}(|Q_{ij}-\tau|\leq s),\mathbb{P}(|\tilde{Q}_{ij}-\tau|\leq s)\lesssim s\sqrt{d}+e^{-cd}. $$

Then, by Markov’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{P}(|Q_{ij}-\tilde{Q}_{ij}|\geq s) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{s^{2}}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{E}(|Q_{ij}-\tilde{Q}_{ij}|^{2})=\frac{1}{s^{2}}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{E}\big(M_{ij}^{2}\big), $$

with $M=Q-\tilde{Q}=X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}+X_{k+1:d}Z^{\mathsf{T}}+ZX_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}$ as in (7.14). We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|M\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|X_{k+1:d}Z^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{n}{d}\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\leq(\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{n}{d})\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim\frac{n}{d}\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2} $$

where in the final bound we used our assumption (2.7) that $\frac{1}{n}\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2}=\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}=o(1/d)$ . Combining with (7.20) yields

$$ |p-\tilde{p}|\lesssim s\sqrt{d}+e^{-cd}+\frac{1}{s^{2}d}\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\,. $$

Optimizing over $s$ gives $s=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/3}$ , which by plugging into the right hand side of our bound, and taking dominant terms yields

$$ |p-\tilde{p}|\lesssim(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/3}+e^{-cd}=o(p),\text{ by }\eqref{assu:gap-gen} $$

as desired.

#### 7.2.3. Proof of Proposition 7.5

$$ \boxed{\begin{aligned} \tilde{B}_{\text{data}}&=p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}+d_{k}p_{1}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\\

#### Proof of Proposition 7.5.

Recall that in this context $B_{\text{spec}}=\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}+d_{k}p_{1}\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ is the rank– $d$ spectral decomposition of the observed adjacency matrix $A$ . Since $\{\tilde{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}=\{\Pi_{X}^{(k)}x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is exactly rank– $k$ , the noisy vectors $\tilde{y}_{i}=\tilde{x}_{i}+z_{i}$ satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 4.1 and the cited proofs depend on the signal only through the parameter estimates in Section 6.2, which remain unchanged after truncation due to Lemma 7.9 and $\tau$ remaining fixed; in particular, we note that coefficients $p_{i}$ in the Gegenbauer expansion $\1(x\geq\tau)=p_{0}+p_{1}x+\dots$ remain the same. $$ \displaystyle d_{k}p_{1}\|\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|B_{\text{spec}}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|A-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|\tilde{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{sph}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|\tilde{B}_{\text{sph}}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+4\|\tilde{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}. \displaystyle\leq\left(2\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{sph}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|\tilde{B}_{\text{sph}}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{\eta}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\right) \displaystyle\qquad+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{\eta}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+4\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Note that the terms inside the parentheses can be controlled via Lemma 6.10, Lemma 6.11 and Lemma 6.14, which combined together give the conclusion of Proposition 4.4. Next $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})$ can be estimated by following the argument in Section 6.4; to find the eigenvalues of $\tilde{B}_{\text{data}},$ we must project away from the first eigenspace, which is spanned by $\zeta$ . To this end, we apply Weyl’s inequality once again:

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{1}(\tilde{A})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{A}) \displaystyle\geq\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})-2\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\geq\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}})-2(\|\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}-\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}). $$

$$ \lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}})=d_{k}p_{1}\lambda_{1}(\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}})=\Theta(dp\tau)\cdot\left(n\mu_{1}^{2}+\tfrac{n}{d}+O(\sqrt{n}\mu_{1})\right)=o(np). $$

The last equality was obtained by (2.5). Then, plugging our estimates on $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\proj})$ , $\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\proj})$ into (7.26) yields $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{A})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{A})\geq\Theta(np)-o(np)$ . Applying this last inequality to (7.25) gives:

$$ \|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{\eta}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\left(1+\frac{\Theta(np)}{\Theta(np)-o(pn)}\right)\lesssim\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Plugging (7.28) into (7.24) and applying Proposition 4.4 to the resultant expression, we obtain

$$ d_{k}p_{1}\|\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim np(\tau^{2}+d\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr\Sigma)\log^{4}n+\max\{np\tau^{2},\sqrt{np}\}\log^{9}n+dp\tau\log^{4}n+\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Finally, applying Proposition 7.6 to the above display, taking dominant terms and dividing by $d_{k}p_{1}=\Theta(dp\tau)$ , produces the desired result. ∎

## 9. Proofs of Application to Random Sampling

### 9.1. Low-rank variant

We begin by stating and proving a low-rank variant of Theorem 2.16, meant as an analogue to Theorem 4.1.

#### Theorem 9.1 (Denoising with low-rank $\Sigma^{\infty}$ ).

With $n,d,p$ as in Theorem 4.1, let $X$ be the matrix whose rows are given by the point cloud $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}$ sampled independently from a distribution $\nu$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , with $\Sigma^{\infty}$ as defined in Definition 2.15 of rank $k$ . Moreover, suppose

$$ \Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}, $$

$$ \esssup_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}, $$

$$ \lambda_{k}(\Sigma^{\infty})=\omega(d^{-1}). $$

Let $G\sim\mathcal{G}_{n,d}(p,\mathcal{X})$ . For the spectral algorithm of Section 2.2, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ :

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lessapprox n\lambda_{1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{1}d}}+\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{k}}\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{dnp}}\right). $$

We prove Theorem 9.1 by applying Theorem 4.1 to $\mathcal{X}$ . Let $\Sigma=\frac{1}{n}X^{\mathsf{T}}X$ and $\{\mu^{2}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ the singular values of $\Sigma$ , as before. We must verify that $\Sigma$ is strictly low rank and that the conditions we impose on $\Sigma^{\infty}$ imply the analogous assumptions (2.5), (2.6), (2.7) on $\Sigma$ in the statement of Theorem 4.1. To this end, we begin by making the informal statement (2.14) precise.

#### Lemma 9.2 (Concentration of $\Sigma$ around $\Sigma^{\infty}$ ).

If $\esssup_{\bf{x}\sim\nu}\|{\bf x}\|_{2}^{2}=O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})$ , then there exists $C\geq 0$ such that with probability at least $1-n^{-11}$

:

$$ \big|\Sigma_{jj}-\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}\big|\leq\|\Sigma-\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\ \ \ \ \forall j:1\leq j\leq d, $$

$$ \bigg|\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma_{jj}-\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}\bigg|\leq C\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\Tr\Sigma_{\infty,\ell:d}}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\ \ \ \ \forall\ell:1\leq\ell\leq d, $$

in particular, setting $\ell=1$ in (9.6) we obtain

$$ \big|\Tr\Sigma-\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\big|\leq C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}. $$

#### Proof.

We begin by proving (9.6). We apply Bernstein’s inequality to

$$ \sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma_{jj}-\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigg(\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}(x_{i})_{j}^{2}-\mathbb{E}\bigg[\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}(x_{i})_{j}^{2}\bigg]\bigg), $$

where $x_{i}\sim\nu$ are i.i.d, and $(x_{i})_{j}$ denotes the $j-$ th coordinate of $x_{i}$ . By (9.2)

$$ \Var\left[\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}(x_{i})_{j}^{2}\right]\leq O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim\nu}\left[\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}(x_{i})_{j}^{2}\right]=O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})\left[\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}\right]. $$

Thus, Bernstein inequality for bounded variables and (9.2) yield (9.6).

Next, we prove (9.5) – in particular, we focus on the second inequality in (9.5) as the first is immediate from the definition of $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . Here we apply matrix Bernstein inequality (e.g.[28, Theorem 5.4.1]) to

$$ \Sigma-\Sigma^{\infty}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}(x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}x_{i}-\Sigma^{\infty}). $$

To do so, we must verify that $\|\frac{1}{n}(x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}x_{i}-\Sigma^{\infty})\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is a bounded random variable. Note that assumption (9.2) implies that

$$ \|x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}x_{i}-\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})^{2} $$

where we used $\|\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}$ . Moreover, the matrix analogue of variance satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\|\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim\nu}\big(x_{i}x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}-\Sigma^{\infty}\big)^{2}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}[\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\big]-(\Sigma^{\infty})^{2}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}(O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})\|\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\big) \displaystyle\leq\frac{O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})^{2}}{n}. $$

Therefore, we obtain

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\|\Sigma-\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\geq t\right)\leq 2d\exp\left(-c\min\bigg\{\frac{t^{2}n}{O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})^{2}},\frac{tn}{O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})}\bigg\}\right). $$

Setting $t=C(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}$ yields the second inequality in (9.5), as desired. ∎

We are now ready check the conditions required for the application of Theorem 4.1 and complete the proof of Theorem 9.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 9.1.

First, we show that if $\Sigma^{\infty}$ is rank $k$ , then $\Sigma$ is at most rank $k$ a.s. Let $u_{1}$ , $\ldots$ , $u_{d}$ denote the eigenbasis for $\Sigma^{\infty}$ with $u_{k+1}$ , $\ldots$ , $u_{d}$ corresponding to the 0 eigenvalue. Then, for $i\geq k+1$

$$ 0=u_{i}^{T}\Sigma^{\infty}u_{i}=\mathbb{E}[u_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\Sigma u_{i}]. $$

Since $\Sigma$ is a positive semidefinite matrix, $u_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\Sigma u_{i}\geq 0$ and the above identity implies $u_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\Sigma u_{i}=0$ a.s. Thus, $\dim\ker\Sigma\geq d-k$ a.s. and the desired conclusion follows.

Next we verify the following conditions (1)–(3), corresponding to (2.5)–(2.7), respectively, hold with high probability.

- (1) $\Tr\Sigma\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}$ : This follows immediately from (9.1) and (9.7).

- (2) The point cloud $\mathcal{X}$ has no outliers ((2.6)) with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ , i.e. $\max_{i,j}\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle=O(\Tr\Sigma)$ : By (9.7) we get that there exists $C\geq 0$ such that with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ (9.8)

$$ \Tr\Sigma\geq\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\left(1-C\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\right). $$

Therefore, letting $n$ be sufficiently large (so that the right side of the above display is positive), we obtain

$$ \max_{i,j}\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\leq\esssup_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})=O(\Tr\Sigma) $$

where the second inequality follows from (9.2).

- (3) $\mu_{k}^{2}=\omega(d^{-1})$ : By Weyl’s inequality and (9.5) we have $\mu_{k}^{2}\geq\lambda_{k}(\Sigma^{\infty})-C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}=\omega(d^{-1}),$ where the last relation follows by (9.3) and (9.1).

Thus, with high probability, Theorem 4.1 applies to $\mathcal{X}$ and (9.4) follows. ∎

To prove Theorem 2.16 we will check that with high probability conditions of Theorem 2.5, in place of Theorem 4.1 as in the proof of Theorem 9.1, are satisfied by the point cloud $\mathcal{X}$ .

### 9.2. Proof of Theorem 2.16

With conditions (1) and (2) as in the proof of Theorem 9.1, these properties hold with high probability by the same argument. To apply Theorem 2.5 it only remains to verify condition (2.7), that $\Sigma$ is numerically low rank, i.e. for some $k=o(\sqrt{d}/\log^{2}n)$ we have that $\mu_{k}\geq\omega(d^{-1/2})$ and $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\leq o\left(\min(p^{3},d^{-1})\right)$ .

#### Lemma 9.3.

Let $x_{1}$ , $\ldots$ , $x_{n}$ denote i.i.d. samples from $\text{Unif}(R\mathcal{S}^{m-1})$ . Then, for $0\leq\varepsilon_{0}\leq\frac{1}{8}$

$$ \bigg|\bigg\{(i,j):i\neq j,|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\geq\frac{\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg\}\bigg|\geq\bigg(1-\sqrt{\frac{96\log n}{(n-1)}}\bigg)\left(1-2\varepsilon_{0}-\frac{1}{m}\right)n(n-1) $$

with probability at least $1-n^{-11}$ .

We begin by recalling that if $U$ is an $m\times m$ orthogonal matrix independent of $x_{i}$ then $Ux_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}x_{i}$ . Thus, if we $U$ satisfies $Ux_{j}=Re_{1}$ we get that

$$ \langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(x_{i})_{1}. $$

Let $g$ denote an $m$ -dimensional standard Gaussian vector. Using (9.15) and the fact that $x_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\frac{Rg}{\|g\|_{2}}$ , for all $\varepsilon\geq 0$ we have that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\leq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg)= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(|(x_{i})_{1}|\leq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(|g_{1}|\leq\frac{\varepsilon\|g\|_{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(|g_{1}|\leq\frac{\varepsilon\|g\|_{2}}{\sqrt{m}},\|g\|_{2}\leq(1+\delta)\sqrt{m}\bigg) \displaystyle+\mathbb{P}\bigg(|g_{1}|\leq\frac{\varepsilon\|g\|_{2}}{\sqrt{m}},\|g\|_{2}\geq(1+\delta)\sqrt{m}\bigg) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|g_{1}|\leq\varepsilon(1+\delta))+\exp(-\delta^{2}m/2) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\varepsilon(1+\delta)+\exp(-\delta^{2}m/2), $$

where the penultimate inequality follows by applying Gaussian concentration to $\|g\|_{2}$ . Setting $\delta=\sqrt{\frac{2\log m}{m}}$ in the above display we get that for $m\geq 2$

$$ \mathbb{P}\bigg(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\leq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg)\leq 2\varepsilon+\frac{1}{m}. $$

Now, using Chernoff bound we get that for $0\leq t\leq 1$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Bigg(\sum_{i,j:j\neq i}\1\left(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\geq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\right)\leq \displaystyle(1-t)\left(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\Bigg)n(n-1)\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j:j\neq i}\1\left(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\geq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\right)\leq(1-t)\left(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\right)(n-1)\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle n\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}\left(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\right)(n-1)\right), $$

and the desired result follows by setting $t=\sqrt{\frac{24\log n}{(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m})(n-1)}}$ and noting that for $m\geq 2$ and $0\leq\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{8}$ we have that $1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\geq\frac{1}{4}.$ ∎

## Appendix A Parameter Estimation Proofs and Asymptotics

With the exception of the proof of Lemma 4.2 in Section A.5, the parameter estimates below are stated and proved for the truncated (strictly rank- $k$ ) model, i.e. in terms of the truncated adjacency matrix $\tilde{A}$ and the associated edge density $\tilde{p}$ . This entails no loss of generality for the numerically low-rank setting of Theorem 2.5. In the strictly rank- $k$ case $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}=0$ , so $\tilde{A}=A$ and $\tilde{p}=p$ . In the numerically low-rank case the tail hypothesis $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}=o\left(\min(p^{3},d^{-1})\right)$ guarantees, via Lemma 7.9, that $p=(1+o(1))\tilde{p}$ , so every estimate proved here for $\tilde{p}$ holds for $p$ up to a $(1+o(1))$ factor and the leading-order asymptotics are unchanged.

### A.1. Proof of Lemma 6.2

Recall the decomposition of the noisy vectors $\tilde{y}_{i}=(a_{i},w_{i})$ where $a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ represents the signal plus noise, and $w_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}$ is the noise. We further decompose the signal vector as $a_{i}=\Pi^{(k)}_{X}x_{i}+N_{i}=\tilde{x}_{i}+N_{i}$ , where $x_{i}$ is the fixed point cloud vector and $N_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{k})$ . The inner product expands as:

$$ \left\langle a_{i},a_{j}\right\rangle=\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},\tilde{x}_{j}\right\rangle+\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle+\left\langle N_{i},\tilde{x}_{j}\right\rangle+\left\langle N_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle. $$

Using Bernstein’s inequality (e.g. see [28, Theorem 2.8.1]), and the fact that for each entry of the vector $N_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ , we have that $\|(N_{i})_{l}\|_{\psi_{2}}=O(1/\sqrt{d})$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left({\exists(i,j)\in[n]^{2},i\neq j:\langle N_{i},N_{j}\rangle\geq t}\right)\leq e^{2\log n-c_{1}\min(td,t^{2}d^{2}/k)}. $$

We require $2\log n<c_{1}\min(td,t^{2}d^{2}/k)$ , so if $k<\log n$ , set $t=C_{1}\frac{\log n}{d}$ , or if $k>\log n$ then $t=C_{1}\frac{\sqrt{k\log n}}{d}$ for some $C_{1}>0$ . Thus, it follows that $\left\langle N_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle\leq C_{1}\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}$ with probability at least $1-n^{-12}$ , for $C_{1}$ sufficiently large uniformly over all pairs $(i,j)\in[n]^{2},i\neq j$ .

By (2.6) and Cauchy-Schwartz,

$$ |\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},\tilde{x}_{j}\right\rangle|\leq\|\tilde{x}_{i}\|_{2}\|\tilde{x}_{j}\|_{2}\leq\|x_{i}\|_{2}\|x_{j}\|_{2}\leq\Tr\Sigma. $$

When $i\neq j$ , the cross-term $\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle$ is a mean zero, Gaussian variable with variance $\|\tilde{x}_{i}\|^{2}/d\lesssim\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)/d$ . Therefore, with probability at least $1-n^{-12}$ , $|\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle|\lesssim\sqrt{\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)\log n/d}$ and thus

$$ \left\langle a_{i},a_{j}\right\rangle=O\left(\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)+\sqrt{\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)\frac{\log n}{d}}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}\right). $$

While it is tempting to bound the right hand side by the simpler expression $O(\Tr\Sigma\cdot\log n)$ (using (2.7)), in some of the arguments below we cannot afford to lose a logarithmic factor.

On the other hand, for the $i=j$ case, the expression (A.1) becomes

$$ \|a_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\tilde{x}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}+2\langle\tilde{x}_{i},N_{i}\rangle+\|N_{i}\|_{2}^{2}. $$

By [28, Theorem 3.1.1], we know that with probability at least $1-n^{-12}$ ,

$$ \|N_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=O\left(\frac{k}{d}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}\right). $$

Applying the condition (2.6) as in the case $i\neq j$ , we obtain

$$ \|a_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=O\left(\Tr\Sigma+\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma\frac{\log n}{d}}+\frac{k}{d}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}}}{d}\right)\leq O(\Tr\Sigma\log n). $$

For the lengths $l_{i}=\|w_{i}\|_{2}$ , note that $d\|w_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\sim\chi^{2}_{d_{k}}$ . $\|\chi_{d_{k}}^{2}-d_{k}\|_{\psi_{1}}=\sqrt{d_{k}}$ , therefore by Bernstein’s inequality,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\exists i\in[n]:|l_{i}^{2}-d_{k}/d|>t\right)\leq e^{\log n-c\min\{\frac{t^{2}d^{2}}{d_{k}},\frac{td}{d_{k}}\}}. $$

Setting $t=C_{3}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}$ for $C_{3}>0$ large enough gives

$$ l_{i}=1+O\left(\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\right). $$

Thus, the product becomes

$$ l_{i}l_{j}=1+O(\sqrt{\log n}/\sqrt{d}). $$

∎

### A.2. Proof of Lemma 6.3

Let $\psi_{X}(t):=\frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}\sum_{i<j}\mathbb{P}(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq t/\sqrt{d})$ , and let $\tau(p)=\tau_{X}(p)$ be the unique value of $\tau$ such that $p=\psi_{X}(\tau\sqrt{d})$ .

#### Lemma A.1.

Let $\Psi(t):=\mathbb{P}(g\geq t)$ denote the complementary distribution function for a standard Gaussian variable on $\mathbb{R}$ . Under the hypotheses of Theorem 2.5,

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{d}\tau_{X}(p) \displaystyle=\Psi^{-1}(p)+O\bigg(\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma+(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n+\frac{\log^{2}n}{\sqrt{d}}\bigg) \displaystyle=\Psi^{-1}(p)+\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma)\,. $$

Note that $\Psi^{-1}(p)=\sqrt{2\log(1/p)}(1+O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}))$ .

Set $\mathcal{E}:=\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma+(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n+\frac{\log^{2}n}{\sqrt{d}}$ . It will suffice to show that for all $i\neq j$ and $T\in[\frac{1}{100},\log n]$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq T/\sqrt{d})=\Psi(T+O(\mathcal{E}))+O(e^{-c\log^{2}n})\,. $$

Indeed, we have that $\psi_{X}$ is strictly decreasing, and from (A.7),

$$ \psi_{X}(T)=\Psi(T+O(\mathcal{E})) $$

for $T\in[\frac{1}{100},\log n]$ . From this and the monotonicity of $\psi_{X}$ and $\Psi$ (noting that $\Psi(\log n)<p<\Psi(\frac{1}{100})$ ) we verify $\sqrt{d}\tau_{X}(p)=\Psi^{-1}(p)+O(\mathcal{E})$ , as desired.

It remains to establish (A.7). By relabeling indices we may assume $(i,j)=(1,2)$ . Letting $g:=\langle z_{1}/\|z_{1}\|_{2},z_{2}\rangle$ , we have

From Cauchy–Schwarz and (2.6) it follows

$$ |\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle|\leq\|x_{1}\|_{2}\|x_{2}\|_{2}\lesssim\Tr\Sigma\,. $$

Next note that $\langle x_{1},z_{2}\rangle\sim N(0,\|x_{1}\|_{2}^{2}/d)$ , so again from (2.6) it follows

$$ \langle x_{1},z_{2}\rangle\lesssim d^{-1/2}(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n $$

with probability $1-O(e^{-c\log^{2}n})$ . The same holds for $\langle x_{2},z_{1}\rangle$ . Finally, since $d\|z_{1}\|_{2}^{2}$ is a sum of independent uniformly sub-exponential variables of expectation 1, we find

$$ \|z_{1}\|_{2}=1+O(\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{d}}) $$

with probability $1-O(e^{-c\log^{2}n})$ . Combining these estimates, we have that

$$ \langle y_{1},y_{2}\rangle=(1+O(\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{d}}))g+O(\Tr\Sigma+d^{-1/2}(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n) $$

with probability $1-O(e^{-c\log^{2}n})$ , from which (A.7) follows. ∎

### A.3. Proof of Lemma 6.4

Before commencing with the proof we recall some facts related to the Gegenbauer polynomial basis.

We will use the random variable $\xi\sim\mathcal{D}_{d}$ , to denote the distribution of $\sqrt{d}\langle u,w\rangle$ where $u$ and $w$ are independent vectors distributed uniformly on the unit sphere $\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ . The scaling factor $\sqrt{d}$ ensures that the second moment is normalized $\mathbb{E}[\xi^{2}]=1$ . The probability density function of $\xi$ is given by

$$ f_{d}(\xi)=\frac{\Gamma(d/2)}{\sqrt{d\pi}\Gamma((d-1)/2)}\left(1-\frac{\xi^{2}}{d}\right)^{\frac{d-3}{2}}. $$

This density function serves as the weight function for the Gegenbauer polynomials $\{q_{k}^{(d)}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ , which form an orthonormal basis for the space $L^{2}([-\sqrt{d},\sqrt{d}],\mathcal{D}_{d})$ such that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{D}_{d}}[q_{k}^{(d)}(\xi)q_{l}^{(d)}(\xi)]=\delta_{kl}. $$

Note that they can be obtained by applying the Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization process to the monomial basis. The Gegenbauer polynomials can be expressed as a linear combination of spherical harmonics, which results in the following identity: for $u,w,v$ independent and uniform in $\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{v}[q_{l}^{(d)}(\sqrt{d}\langle u,v\rangle)q_{j}^{(d)}(\sqrt{d}\langle v,w\rangle)]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{l}^{(d)}}}1_{l=j}q_{l}^{(d)}(\sqrt{d}\langle u,w\rangle). $$

Moreover, from orthonormality, we can obtain that

$$ q_{l}^{(d)}(\sqrt{d})=\sqrt{N_{l}^{(d)}}. $$

We first estimate the size of $\tau^{ij}$ using Lemma 6.3. Recall that the shifted threshold is defined as $\tau^{ij}=(\tau-\left\langle a_{i},a_{j}\right\rangle)/(l_{i}l_{j})$ . Here however, to be more accurate, we use the full estimates on $\langle a_{i},a_{j}\rangle$ without adding extra logarithmic factors, as in the proof of Lemma 6.4. Plugging in the first expression (A.2), and (A.6). Plugging these estimates into the expression for $\tau^{ij}$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\tau^{ij} \displaystyle=\left(\tau-O\left(\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)+\sqrt{\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)\frac{\log n}{d}}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}\right)\right)\left(1+O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}\right)\right)^{-1} \displaystyle=\left(\tau-O\left(\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)+\sqrt{\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)\frac{\log n}{d}}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}\right)\right)\left(1-O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}\right)\right). $$

The last line was obtained by a Taylor expansion. Then, using (2.5) and Lemma 6.3, the dominant term is $\tau^{ij}=\tau+O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log n})$ . Note that the same computation works for $i=j$ since both $\langle a_{i},a_{j}\rangle=O(\Tr\Sigma\log n)$ and $\|a_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=O(\Tr\Sigma\log n)$ from Lemma 6.2.

Recall that $p_{0}^{ij}$ and $p_{1}^{ij}$ correspond to the 0-th and 1-st Gegenbauer coefficients of the expansion of the kernel function $\1(\sqrt{d_{k}}\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{ij})$ , since $\tau^{ij}$ is of the same order of magnitude as in [21], the proof for $p_{0},p_{1}p_{0}^{ij}$ and $p_{1}^{ij}$ follows verbatim as in their Lemma 4.9 [21], which is a direct computation. Throughout this proof, we will condition on the event where the estimates on $l_{i},\langle a_{i},a_{j}\rangle$ in Lemma 6.2 hold. Recall that these events hold with probability at least $1-n^{-12}$ over all pairs $(i,j)\in[n]^{2}$ , including the case when $i=j$ .

$$ L_{i}=l_{i}-1=O(\sqrt{\log(n)/d}) $$

on the same event. Then using the geometric series expansion $(1+x)^{-1}=1-x+O(x^{2})$ for small $x$ , the inverse length is:

$$ l_{i}^{-1}=(1+L_{i})^{-1}=1-L_{i}+O(L_{i}^{2})=1-L_{i}+O\left(\frac{\log n}{d}\right). $$

#### Lemma A.3 (Concentration of degrees).

$$ \mathbb{P}\big(|\deg(i)-r_{i}(y)|\geq t_{i}|z_{i}\big)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{t_{i}^{2}/2}{r_{i}(y_{i})+t_{i}/3}\right)\leq 2n^{-12}. $$

#### Lemma A.4.

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Var(r_{i}(y_{i}))\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[r_{i}(y_{i})^{2}]\leq n\mathbb{E}R. $$

$$ \displaystyle\|R_{3}^{\prime\prime}\|_{\infty} \displaystyle\leq\|aa^{\mathsf{T}}\odot(\1L^{\mathsf{T}}+L\1^{\mathsf{T}})\|_{\infty}+\|\tau\1\1^{\mathsf{T}}\odot(\1L^{\mathsf{T}}+L\1^{\mathsf{T}})\|_{\infty}+\|\tau O(\frac{\log n}{d})\1\1^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\infty} \displaystyle\lesssim O\left(\left(\Tr\Sigma\log n+\tau\right)\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}\right)+\tau O\left(\frac{\log n}{d}\right) \displaystyle\lesssim O\left((\Tr\Sigma\log n+\tau)\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}\right). $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\|R_{3}^{\prime\prime\odot 2}\odot VV^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|R_{3}^{\prime\prime\odot 2}\odot VV^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\|R_{3}^{\prime\prime}\|^{2}_{\infty}\|VV^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\lesssim\underbrace{\left((\Tr\Sigma+\tau)^{2}\frac{\log^{3}n}{d}\right)}_{\eqref{eqn:infty_norm_of_R3''}}\underbrace{\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\right)}_{\text{\lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{fact:spherical_matrix_norm}}} $$

Finally, we combine our estimates (A.48) and (A.50) to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\|R_{3}^{\prime}\odot VV^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2(1+O\left(\frac{\log n}{d}\right))\|aa^{\mathsf{T}}\odot R_{3}^{\prime\prime}\odot VV^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|R_{3}^{\prime\prime\odot 2}\odot VV^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim(1+O\left(\frac{\log n}{d}\right))\big[(\Tr\Sigma\log n)^{2}+\tau\Tr\Sigma\log n\big]O\left(\frac{n\sqrt{\log n}}{d\sqrt{d}}\right)+\left((\Tr\Sigma+\tau)^{2}\right)\left(\frac{n{\log^{3}n}}{d\sqrt{d}}\right) \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{n}{d^{3/2}}\tau^{2}\log^{3}n. $$

The last line was obtained using Lemma 6.3 in conjunction with (2.5). ∎
